The act of removing impurities, negative energy, stagnation, and unwanted influences from a person, place, object, or situation. Purification is one of the most essential and frequently performed actions in all magickal practice. It prepares the stage for every other working.

Why Purify?

Everything accumulates energy over time. A new tool from a shop carries the energy of everyone who handled it. A room where an argument took place holds residual tension. Even your own energy field picks up influences from the people and places you encounter daily. Purification strips away these accumulated layers, returning the target to a neutral, clean state that is ready to receive fresh intention.

Purification is also the essential first step in ritual preparation. Cleansing yourself, your tools, and your space before spellwork ensures that lingering energies do not interfere with your intention.

Common Methods of Purification

Different methods suit different situations. Always choose a technique that will not physically damage the object or harm the person being cleansed:

  • Smoke cleansing involves passing an object through incense smoke or the smoke of a smudge bundle. The smoke carries away stagnant energy
  • Water cleansing involves sprinkling, aspersing, or submerging in ritually prepared water such as Holy Water, Moon Water, or salt water. Only suitable for items that can safely withstand moisture
  • Salt is a powerful absorber of negative energy. Items can be placed on or buried in salt, or salt can be sprinkled around a space
  • Sound from singing bowls, bells, clapping, drumming, or chanting breaks up stagnant energy through vibration. Effective for large spaces and situations where smoke or water would be impractical
  • Sunlight and Moonlight can purify objects placed in direct light for a period of time. Sunlight purifies with active, fiery energy while moonlight purifies with gentle, receptive energy
  • Earth burial allows the earth to absorb and neutralize unwanted energy from items buried in soil
  • Breath involves deliberately breathing across an object with the intention to cleanse. Simple, requires no tools, and can be done anywhere

Purification in Ritual Work

Before beginning any magickal working, most practitioners perform some form of purification. This might be as simple as washing your hands with intention, or as elaborate as a full ritual bath with herbs and oils. The key is not the complexity of the method but the clarity of your intention to cleanse.

After workings, especially intense or emotionally heavy ones, purification helps you return to your baseline state. Ground first to release excess energy, then cleanse to clear any residual influences.

The Fire Element Connection

Fire and Water both share strong ties to purification. Fire purifies through transformation, burning away impurities and reducing things to their essence. Water purifies through washing, dissolving and carrying away what no longer serves. The method you choose often depends on whether the situation calls for fire's decisive intensity or water's gentle persistence.

Regular Cleansing Practice

Purification is not a one time event. Many practitioners build regular cleansing into their routines: a weekly smoke cleanse of their home, a monthly ritual bath, or a daily visualization of unwanted energy draining away. Consistent purification prevents the buildup of stagnant energy and keeps your practice space vibrant and clear.

  • Violet, white violet specifically
  • Palm, specifically Coconut (coconut palm) and Dragon's Blood (dragon's blood palm)
  • Chamomile, tagged as both German Chamomile and Roman Chamomile

🐟Reviving Reciprocity
↗Symbols1
6

Magick operates as an exchange of powers. Consistently effective practice requires more than personal desire: the universe does not exist solely to serve the practitioner. There is always an exchange of energy, an exchange of gifts. Magick is about mutually satisfying relationships between forces and powers, including but not limited to the practitioner's own.

The Principle

When seeking something from a power, offer something in return. When receiving a gift or favor, give one back. This maintains the balance of power in the universe. In many cases, reciprocity is not merely courteous but necessary.

Practical Applications

  • Botanicals work more powerfully for a practitioner who reciprocates by offering libations when harvesting
  • Spirits will often decline to work with someone who does not provide payment of some kind, which may be as simple as sustained devotion or as complex as a specific ritual, depending on the spirit
  • Favors received create an expectation of return offerings, maintaining the ongoing relationship between practitioner and power

Why It Matters

Power and favors must be balanced. The practitioner is as much a contributor to the universe as a receiver of its bounties. Neglecting reciprocity weakens the magickal relationship over time and may result in spirits or forces withdrawing their assistance entirely.

Origins

Scrying at its most fundamental is divination via a smooth surface. The practice may have originated when someone gazing into a calm lake surface fell into a trance and received visions or psychic impressions. Because lakes are not always accessible or reliably still, practitioners developed other surfaces and vessels that could be prepared on demand.

Among the oldest known depictions of scrying are ancient images of Kybele, the Magna Mater, holding and gazing into a pan of water. This method remains as effective as ever. Its primary requirement is patience and the capacity to quiet the mind: this is not a quick or spontaneous method. The mind needs time and openness to settle into receptivity.

Water scrying methods are particularly well-suited to those born under the astrological water signs of Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, as well as Aquarius.

Simple Methods

Lake or natural water: If a genuinely tranquil lake or other smooth body of water is accessible, sitting beside it and gazing into the still surface remains one of the most effective scrying methods available. Allow the mind to become still and simply observe what arises.

Black ink: A small shallow dish filled with black ink can serve as a scrying surface. Some practitioners find the stillness and depth of black ink especially conducive to visioning. Gaze into the ink to receive the oracle.

Scrying is a meditative form of psychic visioning that uses a physical focal point to receive information. Unlike pure meditation, scrying gives your conscious mind something to engage with while your intuitive awareness opens.

Protective Applications

Scrying can be used to detect threats to yourself, your home, your family, or others. Its visionary nature makes it well-suited for uncovering hidden dangers or perceiving situations that haven't yet manifested physically.

Tools for Scrying

Different tools may yield different results, experiment to find what works best for you:

  • Candle flame, the flickering light provides natural movement for the eye to follow
  • Bowl of water, a classic scrying surface; dark bowls work particularly well
  • Bowl of salt or sand, can be observed visually or interacted with by running fingers through it
  • Crystal, crystal balls, spheres, or clear points serve as focal objects
  • Incense smoke, the rising, shifting patterns offer constantly changing imagery

Basic Technique

Setting: Work in a darkened room with low, ambient music if desired.

Entering trance: Allow yourself to slip into a trancelike state. If you struggle with stillness in traditional meditation, scrying offers an excellent alternative, there can be movement, chanting, singing, humming, or gentle rocking. The only requirements are you and the information.

For beginners: Start with a bowl of salt or sand. Run your fingers over the surface or gently toss the grains until your thinking mind quiets and your symbolic understanding activates. This tactile engagement helps bridge the gap between conscious awareness and intuitive reception.

Dream Grimoire

Dream Techniques

Flashbulb Memory and Dream Recall

Vivid dreams imprint on memory like flashbulb memories, those photographic snapshots of significant moments (Princess Diana's death, 9/11). These dreams persist with clarity. Most dreams fade within minutes as daily life intrudes. The conscious mind tidies details, rationalizing or explaining away uncomfortable experiences.

Dreams contain hidden information. Recalling them clarifies unresolvable choices and reveals patterns in daily occurrences. Regular recording increases spontaneous recall.

Techniques for Dream Recall

Immediate Capture

Keep a notebook and pen at your bedside or use your phone. Write down details immediately upon waking, whether midnight or morning. Record dream characters from daily life and emotional responses to scenarios. This takes one minute and helps you return to sleep free from the dream.

Returning to Pleasant Dreams

Picture the last or strongest pleasurable image. Imagine a path leading back to that place in the dream.

Calming After Nightmares

Visualize floating on fluffy pink clouds through a starlit sky or wrapped in a warm, dark blanket.

Bad Dreams as Diagnostic Tools

Bad dreams highlight oversights needing remedy or unfinished business. A tire burst on the freeway signals real tire pressure issues or distracted driving habits, not psychic warnings. Anxiety dreams where everything fails indicate stress overload. They signal time to step back.

Rewriting Dream Endings

A spiral symbolizes cyclic development, indicating the ebbs and flows of life. It indicates that you should go with the flow, rather than fighting it.

Visualize the point where things went wrong. Consciously change the ending in your semi-waking state. This transfers successful crisis-management energy to waking life. This technique works particularly well for negative past-life dreams.

Dream Incubation

Ancient Egyptians pioneered dream direction, using sleep to answer questions. The creative, inspirational mind operates largely unconsciously. Sleep reveals solutions the logical brain missed. Egyptian priests used dream temples. Ordinary people sat in dark spaces watching oil lamp light to relax before sleep.

Method for Question Dreams

Place lavender oil beneath your pillow. In total darkness, light a battery-operated candle, nightlight, or shaded lamp. Recite your question or area needing guidance seven times softly and continuously. Half close your eyes. Focus on the halo around the light. Recite the question seven more times, quieter each repetition until words fade to silence. Extinguish the light. Sleep while visualizing yourself walking into the golden light.

The answer arrives in the dream, often symbolically. If not, repeat the next night. Within two or three attempts, the answer comes. With experience, you may only need to recite the question before sleep or write it down and place it under your pillow.

Lucid Dreaming

Becoming aware that you are dreaming while still asleep opens a doorway to conscious exploration. Most people wake themselves immediately at this realization, cutting short the opportunity for insight. The key is staying calm and remaining in the dream state once lucidity arrives.

Working with Spontaneous Lucidity

When you realize you are dreaming, consciously ask the dream to show you something relevant to your current life situation. Direct it to take you somewhere helpful. Observe everything with deliberate attention. Notice colors, objects, people, emotions, and spatial details. Stay in the scene as long as possible before releasing it.

You can choose to wake after the experience or return to normal sleep. Either way, the lucid dream remains accessible to memory.

Think about the dream before getting out of bed. When you rise, immediately record the experience. Note colors specifically, as they carry symbolic weight. Write down the emotions you felt. Insights may surface as you write. Later, review your notes when you have time to reflect. The message may be obvious or require interpretation through color symbolism and recurring dream patterns.

Methods to Induce Lucid Dreams

Alarm Clock Interruption

Set an alarm for four hours after falling asleep. Wake just enough to turn it off, then return to sleep. You will often reenter the dream you were having. Once inside, you can direct where it goes.

Pre-Sleep Intention

Tell yourself before sleep that you will experience a lucid dream tonight. Practice this on weekends or days when you do not need to wake to an alarm, as the most valuable reflection time comes immediately upon waking. Rushed mornings erase dream memory.

Reality Check Trigger

Choose a specific element (your hands, a door, a mirror) and repeatedly tell yourself throughout the day and before sleep: "When I see my hands in a dream, I will know I am dreaming." This plants a recognition trigger in your unconscious mind.

Dream Reentry

If you wake early remembering a dream, relax and let yourself drift back into it. Once you are inside the dream again, begin steering its direction.

Building Lucid Awareness Through Visualization

Create your ideal dream scene before sleep: a tropical shore, lakeside house, castle, or palace. Cast yourself as the central character. Imagine detailed interactions like walking through golden palace rooms or swimming with multicolored fish.

Create a symbol to trigger lucidity. Choose something exotic and memorable: a rainbow-colored bird, gigantic multicolored butterfly, golden peacock studded with gems. Rerun the dream scene mentally, letting the symbol appear five or six times. Say to yourself: "When I see the multicolored butterfly, I will know I am dreaming and anything is possible."

Drift to sleep focusing on the image. Be patient. The first night you may see only fragments or nothing. You may not recall you are dreaming. Repeat nightly until you see the symbol or recognize you are dreaming during sleep.

Visit wherever and whoever you want, past, present, or future. Rehearse conversations you need to have in waking life. Overcome obstacles and adversaries. Change nightmare endings by confronting what frightens you. Wake refreshed and powerful.

Consistency and Patience

No method works every time. Celebrate lucid dreams when they happen, but do not become discouraged when they do not. The capacity builds with practice.

Psychic Dreams

In dreams, time and space barriers weaken. Logic no longer dominates awareness. Unconscious radar replaces conscious thought, offering warnings about coming events. This helps avert hazards or seize opportunities. Parents and children link telepathically in sleep. New parents receive alerts to child distress.

Distinguishing Predictive Dreams

True predictive dreams feel more real than vivid dreams. They persist long after ordinary dreams fade. The scene appears three-dimensional and detailed. Upon waking, you feel fully alert, not sleepy or confused. These dreams can connect twin souls on the dream plane, drawing you to the place where you will meet.

Regular anxiety dreams involve nagging worry rather than urgency. They signal general life jitters. Trusting dreams reduces anxiety.

Deceased Visitors

Deceased family members most commonly appear in dreams. A grandmother or grandfather visiting in sleep offers comfort, not fear. This may heal grief. If the relation died years ago, such dreams recall childhood love and reassurance during vulnerable periods.

Some believe a person's essential personality survives death and communicates through dreams. When you could not say goodbye or the relative died with unresolved conflict, dreams bring reconciliation. Afterward, most people feel profound peace, especially when death came suddenly or after prolonged suffering.

Past Life Dreams

Past-life or ancestral-memory dreams reveal sources of current phobias and paths to overcome them. When you know nothing of your heritage (through adoption, for example), dreams rekindle clues to severed connections. These can be explored in waking life if ancestors or unknown living relatives seek contact.

Dreams as Life Tools

Dreams reveal hidden patterns. Key life periods activate psychic powers: pregnancy, childhood, adolescence, the twenties and thirties, bereavement, sorrow, times of major change. Dreams transform the sleep plane into a treasure trove of potential.

Dreams make sense of the world, unencumbered by mundane limitations that constrain waking life. Edgar Cayce said: "Dreams are today's answers to tomorrow's questions."

Dream Pillows

Dream pillows are botanical sachets placed under the cheek or beside the pillow during sleep. The pillow's power is delivered through its aroma. Possible uses include basic dream stimulation, incubating specific types of dreams (erotic, financial, or otherwise), sleep enhancement, nightmare prevention, and spiritual protection during sleep. Tailor the blend to your intention by selecting botanicals that correspond to your desired outcome.

Crafting a dream pillow is a spell. Charge and consecrate materials as you work. Focus on your intention throughout, and treat each knot tied as an opportunity for a separate knot spell.

Standard dimensions: 12 inches × 8 inches (30 cm × 20 cm), filled with approximately 8–10 oz (300 g) of dried herbs. A flat, loosely filled pillow is more comfortable and more effective than an overstuffed one.

Basic Dream Pillow Construction

  1. Botanicals must be completely dry before sewing into the pillow. Damp material may rot and produce a foul fragrance that stimulates nightmares rather than dreams.
  2. Unless very soft, grind ingredients to a fine powder. Rose petals are preferable to buds (which are pointy). Bay leaves must be at least crushed before use.
  3. If adding essential or fragrance oils, blend them thoroughly into the dried material with a twig or wooden chopstick. Allow to dry completely before sewing.
  4. If adding charms or harder roots, place them carefully in the center and surround with softer material.
  5. The fragrance should be pleasing or at minimum neutral. Dislike of a botanical's aroma may signal it is not suited for you. Note that fragrance is more intense in the dark, deprived of other sensory stimulation. Adjust accordingly.

Crystal Dream Pillows

Crystals enhance dreaming but must be cleansed periodically and after disturbing dreams. Do not sew them permanently inside a pillow.

  1. Place a crystal on a clean white handkerchief together with dream herbs.
  2. Tie together with a blue silk ribbon.
  3. Sleep with this under your pillow or cheek.
  4. Remove and cleanse the crystal as needed.

Doctoring a Commercial Dream Pillow

Commercially made dream pillows often have beautiful fabric but weak botanical stuffing. Enhance them:

  1. Carefully open the seams and remove the herbs.
  2. Dress the original herbs with dream-enhancing oil and allow them to dry before replacing, or substitute fresh herbs of your choice.
  3. Sew the bag back up and enjoy it.

Dream Incense: General Method

Dream incense is not burned while you sleep. The burning process should be complete just prior to going to bed.

  1. Close doors and windows before lighting the incense to intensify its effects and fragrance.
  2. Place the incense burner on a nightstand or in a safe area near the bed.
  3. Burn the incense completely.
  4. When the incense has fully burned, open doors and/or windows to provide ventilation, then go to sleep. Do not wait too long after ventilating or the fragrance may dissipate.

Flower Essence Remedies for Dream Stimulation

Flower essence remedies work upon the soul and emotions, the very layers of experience most readily expressed through dreams. The effects of any flower essence may surface through dreaming, but the following have been specifically identified as stimulating and facilitating the dream process:

  • Apple (FES)
  • Chokecherry (Pegasus)
  • Gum Plant / Grindelia (FES)
  • Jimson Weed / Datura (Pegasus)
  • Mugwort (FES, Pegasus)

Take in combinations of up to six remedies at a time, following the manufacturer's directions. Place a few drops into a glass of spring water and drink before going to sleep, or rub the flower remedies into the thin skin between your thumb and forefinger.

Dream Divination

Ancestors communicate through dreams. This page covers how ancestral dreaming works, how to stimulate and record dreams, how to interpret dream symbols, and a traditional Neapolitan ritual for incubating a specific question.

Ancestors & Dreams

Dreams often begin to shift once an ancestor veneration practice is established. Follow-up dreams after rituals honoring ancestors are common. Dreaming tends to become more intense when ancestors are actively trying to reach someone. The relationship is reciprocal.

After receiving a particularly powerful dream, a small ritual of acknowledgment can be meaningful:

  • Wear a piece of clothing that appeared in the dream.
  • Visit a place of power, a river or a crossroads, and offer a prayer of thanksgiving.
  • Light a candle on the ancestor altar.

Stimulating & Recording Dreams

Dream Stimulation

Herbal teas (such as dandelion) and tinctures (such as California poppy) may help stimulate dreaming. For those who prefer not to ingest anything, one of the most effective techniques is simply committing to journaling dreams.

Keeping a Dream Journal

  • Keep a dedicated journal on the nightstand.
  • Setting an extra alarm a few hours before the usual wake time can disrupt the sleep cycle and improve dream recall.
  • When recording a dream, note: calendar date, astrological conditions, lunar phase, and (if applicable) menstrual cycle position.
  • Review journal entries regularly. Patterns emerge over time. Specific ancestors may arrive during particular lunar phases or when the moon is in a certain zodiac sign.

Bibliomancy with the Dream Journal

The dream journal can also be used for bibliomancy (book divination): say a prayer, ask a question, and flip to a random page. Interpret whatever line appears in light of that question.

Interpreting Dream Symbols

There is no universal set of dream symbols. Meaning is personal, relational, and contextual.

Using a dream dictionary:

  • Choose one book and stay with it consistently.
  • Skim through it before needing it for a specific dream. Even just reading a few entries after prayers at the altar helps open the channel between ancestors, the unconscious mind, and waking awareness.
  • Freudian psychoanalysis and Jungian psychoanalysis each produce different symbolic languages; dreamers tend to dream in the symbolic vocabulary of whatever system they are most exposed to.

Trusting your own interpretation:

External authorities are never required. Dreams often seem random or meaningless immediately upon waking, but rereading them later, especially when alert but not yet fully immersed in daily life, tends to surface intuitive connections between dream symbols and current waking circumstances.

Neapolitan Dream Incubation Ritual

In the folk tradition of southern Italy and Sicily, specific questions may be brought to ancestors or saints through ritual prayer, with the response received through an omen or a dream. The following is a Neapolitan example, courtesy of scholar and teacher Anna Scognamiglio:

  1. Make the Sign of the Cross three times.
  2. Recite the following three times, then ask your question:
"Ogge è luna, dimane è marte, 'a sciorta mia stanotte parte, parte e fa nu luongo cammino, vieneme nsuonno sciorta bella mia."

(Translation: "Today is Moon, tomorrow is Mars, my destiny tonight leaves, leaves and takes a long walk, come into my dream my beautiful destiny.")

  1. Recite three Hail Marys.
  2. Repeat steps 1–3 three times total.
  3. End with three Signs of the Cross.

At midnight, go to a window or balcony and watch for a sign from the street:

  • A dog barking: a good sign.
  • A cat meowing: a bad sign.
  • People talking: a common omen; interpret their words in light of the question.

If no omens appear, a dream will typically come that night.

Entity Grimoire

Offerings

The practice of making offerings forms the third pillar of daily magickal work, alongside meditation and banishing. Where banishing rituals protect through force, offerings protect through peace, extending an olive branch to spirits and elemental forces that share the world.

Why Make Offerings

Human activity can negatively impact the spiritual dimension. Building on sacred ground, polluting natural spaces, or disturbing power spots may provoke local guardians and forces to act in retribution. In traditional cultures, shamans serve as mediators, mending these breaches and maintaining harmony between worlds. Through offerings, the practitioner signals that any harm was unintentional and seeks to make amends.

Beyond protection, offerings are powerful tools for gaining spiritual allies and manifesting magickal work. Regular offerings build bonds with spiritual forces, making the universe more willing to support your practice.

Types of Offerings

Offerings can be physical or mental, though most spirits feed on subtle essence rather than physical substance itself. The exception is smoke from burnt substances. Many spirits take nourishment directly from incense, herbs, and woods. Even with solid offerings like cakes and alcohol, you can amplify their power by mentally multiplying them through will, seeing them fill infinite space.

Informal Offerings

  • A dime or whiskey left on a grave
  • Flowers or water poured near a tree
  • Incense burned and mentally offered to the ten directions

These small acts of generosity build good relationships with spiritual forces around your home and wherever you travel.

Formal Offerings

For structured practice, see the complete ritual below. This working rewards protectors and familiars who assist you while pacifying spirits that might cause obstacles. It speaks to elemental and spirit forces generally, making it safe for regular practice.

Cultural Considerations

When making offerings to specific classes of spirits, research is essential. Certain offerings can offend particular beings:

  • Salt upsets the dead in some Afro-Caribbean traditions
  • Meat enrages Nagas in Himalayan practices

Let research, omens, and dreams guide your offerings to specific entities.

Daily Practice

The ideal magickal regimen includes meditation, banishing, and offerings. Aim for meditation and banishing daily (preferably twice), with offerings at least once weekly. These practices take little time once learned and provide the foundation for all other magickal work.

Ancestor Offerings

In many respects, ancestor veneration is an adaptation of the way love is expressed among the living, adjusted for the circumstances of the dead. Four of Gary Chapman's five archetypal love languages apply directly: spending quality time, words of affirmation, acts of service, and exchanging gifts. Offerings are the gift-giving dimension of that relationship.

The Spirit of Offering

The difference between placing a morsel of food on a plate and making an offering lies in the quality of attention and feeling brought to the act. Offerings made with genuine joy, the selfless kind associated with giving rather than receiving, carry more power than those made out of obligation or habit.

Why Give Offerings to Ancestors

  • Sustenance: In many traditions, the souls of the dead require food and other offerings to remain strong. Without regular nourishment, spirits weaken and eventually fade. Consistent offerings empower the ancestors to work on behalf of the lineage.
  • Communication: Offerings form a symbolic language. The specific items chosen signal intent: coffee implies it is time to work, engage, or discuss; champagne signals celebration. Choosing the right offering sharpens the message and strengthens the petition. A spell is, in this sense, a prayer in three dimensions: the physical ingredients reinforce the spoken petition and ground it in the material world.
  • Thanksgiving: Offerings are given in gratitude when ancestors have interceded. The reciprocity principle applies: give in proportion to what has been received. Lavish gifts offered before lavish gifts have been given can create energetic imbalance. Aim for balance.

A Caution Regarding Ghosts

Offerings should not be given to ghosts. Doing so empowers them and may increase disruption. If a ghost's presence is felt, the appropriate response is prayer for their peace and healing. Through sustained loving prayer, a ghost may eventually rehabilitate and become a true ancestor; at that point, offerings become appropriate.

Food and Meals

Sharing food is among the simplest, least expensive, and most powerful offerings available. A small portion of whatever is being eaten, not a full serving, is offered to the ancestors before the living eat. In African Diasporic traditions, food and drink at religious events are offered to the ancestors first as a matter of course. This creates a bond between the living and the dead: both are, in a sense, seated at the same table.

Cooking as Ritual Devotion

Cooking is alchemy: heat transforms raw materials drawn from the earth into something entirely new. The time spent cooking a meal that will be shared with the ancestors is itself a form of service and devotion, independent of the quality of the result. Learning ancestral recipes, dishes favored by recently deceased relatives, or traditional foods from the regions ancestors inhabited all deepen the relationship. The learning itself counts.

Learning to cook regional, seasonal foods from the area where the practitioner currently lives grounds the ancestral line by putting them in contact with local land spirits. Some nutritionists observe that a healthy diet blends ancestral foods with locally seasonal ones. A prayer of welcome and thanksgiving the first time a new seasonal fruit or vegetable crosses the threshold is a natural extension of this practice.

At Gatherings

Any social gathering tends to attract ancestral spirits. Serving the ancestors a small portion of each dish before serving living guests reflects the etiquette of formal dinners, where honored guests are served first. The ancestors are, by definition, the oldest guests present and merit acknowledgment, even if the gesture is small and private.

Eating Away From Home

For those who eat outside the home frequently, pushing a small bite to the side of the plate and mentally recognizing it as an offering to the ancestors is a valid practice.

Specific Offerings and Their Uses

OfferingWhen to UseNotes
Coffee / TeaWhen quick action or intervention is needed; to accompany a petitionStimulants that "wake the ancestors up" and prompt them to get working
BreadGeneral veneration; reaching older generations of the lineageAssociated with life and divinity across cultures for ~30,000 years; connected to Demeter, the Eucharist, and the civilizing of humanity through grain cultivation
Ancient Beverages (wine, beer, sake, mead)Connecting with initiated or tradition-holding ancestors; deep lineage workResearch historically appropriate beverages for the lineage; locally brewed or home-brewed options are also valid. Avoid if alcohol is a source of harm in the family.
FlowersGeneral altar keeping; attracting benevolent spiritsWhite roses and lilies are all-purpose. Flowers the ancestor preferred in life are meaningful. The Victorian language of flowers (see Phillips' Floral Emblems or Shoberl's The Language of Flowers) can be used for symbolic communication.
SweetsThanksgiving after a favor is granted; sweetening petitions (new job, promotion, favor-seeking)Contrast with coffee/tea: sweets come after, stimulants come before
Hard LiquorHonoring specific ancestors; lineage-specific workOffer whatever a particular ancestor preferred in life, or a regionally significant spirit. Old herbal liqueurs (absinthe, Chartreuse, amaro) contain medicinal herbs and are good offerings for continued health. Omit if alcoholism affected the line.
TobaccoHonoring ancestors who used tobacco; specific petitionsCan be offered loose on a plate, or as a lit or unlit cigarette/cigar. Omit if smoking-related illness affected the line.
Toiletries (perfume, soap, cologne)Refreshment; attracting benevolent spiritsFlorida Water, Hoyt's Cologne, Kolonia 1800, and Kananga Water are traditional in African-American and Afro-Caribbean practice. Kananga Water is specifically associated with the ancestors.
IncenseDaily practice; drawing spirits; sustenanceIn traditional Chinese practice, incense is lit at the ancestor altar daily. In other traditions it is a medium for attracting and manifesting spirits. Frankincense, myrrh, and church incense (a blend of the two) are commonly used.

Ex Votos

Ex votos (ex voto suscepto: "from the vow made") are special offerings promised at the time a petition is made and given only if the petition is granted. The practice goes back to the ancient world and continues in Catholic and Greek Orthodox traditions, where ex votos typically take the form of paintings depicting the favor received or small sculptures in metal or wax.

Body-part shapes are especially common and map symbolically to the nature of the petition:

FormPetition
FeetGrounding during difficulty; protection while traveling; guidance when lost
HandsWork, influence, and practical matters
EyesFreedom from deception; insight; divination and psychic ability
BrainIntelligence; passing exams; mental challenges
LungsInspiration
HeartLove; emotional healing; affairs of the heart

Personal symbolic connections are valid. An ex voto is meant to capture the feeling of answered prayer; there is no wrong way to express that through a personal symbol.

Tools

Small tools or toy replicas of tools can be given as offerings, serving as a symbolic empowerment that gives the ancestors additional strength for a specific type of working. Unlike ex votos, which are given in response to a fulfilled petition, tools can be given as general encouragement.

ToolUse
CompassGuidance; direction when feeling lost
WeaponsProtection
FanCooling a heated situation
Musical instrumentRestoring joy and zest for life in times of despair
ScalesJustice and equality
Carpentry toolsEmployment; fixing what is broken
Sewing toolsPeace and harmony in the home
Magickal toolsInvoking ancestral support for occult and magickal practice

How to Give Offerings

Frequency

How often offerings are given is a matter of personal relationship with the ancestors. Some practitioners give offerings once a year on a day traditionally devoted to ancestor veneration (All Souls' Day, the Hungry Ghost Festival) or on a personally significant date (a birthday, an anniversary of someone's passing). Others find a daily rhythm more natural. There is no wrong answer; follow intuition and observe how the practice feels over time.

Before divination or magickal work, making an offering while praying for ancestral blessing is especially recommended.

Frequency by Offering Type

  • Tools and ex votos — Given sparingly and left permanently. It would be discourteous to take back a gift. Because altars grow over time, avoid accumulating clutter; give these only when genuinely moved to do so.
  • Consumable offerings (food, beverage) — Ideally left on the altar overnight, or at minimum until a candle lit alongside them has burned down. Remove before they become moldy.

Disposal

Most offerings can be disposed of in the trash. If something unusual is noticed (a pest found dead in the offering, an unexplained smell or discoloration), dispose of it in a more intentional way: bring it to a crossroads or drop it into running water.

Discernment

If a particular offering seems unwelcome, perhaps because it was taboo within a significant branch of the lineage, that is useful information. Note it and adjust. It is unlikely to cause lasting harm. The ancestors are invested in the relationship and generally patient with honest mistakes.

Journal Prompts: Offerings

  1. The five love languages are: spending quality time together, words of affirmation, acts of service, physical touch, and exchanging gifts. Which do you prefer to use to show love to others? Which do you prefer others use to show love to you? (This prompt is especially fruitful when explored with family members and romantic partners.)
  2. What is the best gift you have ever received? What made it so meaningful?
  3. How do you feel about cooking? If confidence in the kitchen is lacking, what is one small step that might help build it?
  4. Looking back at your list of blood and lineage ancestors:
    • Do you know what any of these ancestors' favorite foods were?
    • Did any of them live through famine or the Great Depression? Do you see patterns in your living family's relationship with food that might trace back to those experiences?
  5. What do you know about your ancestral foodways? What stories have you heard about your ancestral foods? Are there any foods from your ancestral tradition that you feel a particular affinity for?
  6. What do you know about the local, seasonal foods from the land you currently live on? What stories have you heard about them? Do you feel a particular affinity for any?
  7. What fermented beverages were loved by your ancestors? How do you feel about drinking alcohol? Does it feel more like medicine or poison to you?

Working With Spirits

The relationship between practitioner and spirit defines the work more than any ritual structure. Where space exists, awareness manifests as varied classes of beings with different natures and powers. Some are localized, some are not. Some speak using only information within your mind to express themselves, others communicate as clearly as a person standing before you. Some influence the material world, some do not.

Psychological vs. Traditional Views

Modern practitioners often interpret spirits as psychological projections, aspects of the practitioner's own mind rather than independent entities. This view suggests spells provide self-empowerment and mystery rather than direct influence on external reality.

This psychological framework limits both perception and results. The assumption that spirits exist only as projected aspects of individual psyches reduces ceremony to theater rather than genuine contact with external intelligence.

The Traditional Approach

Ancient grimoires were written for their rituals to be performed as if the spirit were a separate, discarnate intelligence. Even if you personally believe spirits are psychological constructs, treating them as separate entities during ceremony produces better results. If the mechanism is belief-based psychology, believing more strongly in the spirit's independent existence creates stronger results than treating the work as a mental trick.

Experience across traditions supports the view that spirits are independent intelligences. Some interface with human consciousness to communicate, but they are not limited to or contained by individual human minds. They act in ways that exceed the boundaries of psychological projection.

Working with Spirit Authority

Authority and Will

The most elaborate traditional rites fail if the practitioner lacks knowledge of their true will and access to higher powers. Successful spirit work depends on the practitioner's spiritual authority and connection to divine forces, not on ritual complexity alone. Faith that divine will manifests through the practitioner is what wins confrontations with hostile entities and earns respect from allied spirits.

Practical Considerations

Treat spirits in ritual according to traditional frameworks regardless of your personal metaphysical beliefs. This approach has been tested across centuries and produces consistent results.

Etiquette for Working with Spirits

Certain rules apply when working with spirit helpers, as in any relationship:

  • Ask for assistance - Guides, guardians, and deities respect your free will and may not intervene unless invited to do so.
  • Show respect - Treat spirit helpers as honored teachers and allies, not servants.
  • Avoid micromanaging - When seeking aid from spirit beings, turn over the reins and allow them to carry out your request as they see fit.
  • Do not seek help for harmful purposes - Benevolent spirits will not support harmful causes, and you do not want to attract malevolent entities.
  • Express gratitude - Thank the beings who assist you and consider giving them an offering.

Ways to Attract Divine Assistance

Deities may come to you in dreams, meditation, or visions. Throughout history, countless people have experienced visitations from divine beings. Such appearances can happen to anyone, anytime.

If spontaneous contact does not occur, other methods can catch a deity's attention:

  • Research thoroughly - Learn as much as possible about the deity you wish to attract through myths, spiritual literature, and folklore.
  • Create a dedicated altar - Set up and dedicate an altar to your chosen deity.
  • Display sacred imagery - Collect and display artwork depicting the deities you wish to petition in a prominent place.
  • Make appropriate offerings - Discover what specific deities prefer (particular plants, foods, stones) and place these on your altar or in a special outdoor location.
  • Stay receptive - Keep an open mind and heart when working with deities. Trust your intuition to tune into higher frequencies.
  • Cultivate belief - Trust that spirits will communicate with you. Doubt closes the door between you and magickal beings. When dealing with supernatural forces, you'll see it when you believe it.

Guardian Spirits Across Traditions

Guardian spirits serve as protectors, guides, and intermediaries between the practitioner and higher powers. Different traditions conceptualize and work with guardian spirits in distinct ways.

Tibetan Buddhism works with dharmapalas (wrathful protector deities) who defend practitioners and the dharma itself. These fierce guardians like Palden Lhamo and the Eight Dharma Protectors require empowerment from qualified teachers and ongoing devotional relationships.

Catholic and folk Catholic traditions invoke saints as guardian spirits. Practitioners develop relationships through prayer, offerings of candles and flowers, and petitions for specific forms of protection or aid. Saints act as intermediaries who carry prayers to higher divine authority.

Vodou and related African diasporic traditions work with loa as guardian spirits. The Met Tet (master of the head) serves as the primary guardian loa for each practitioner. Relationships with loa require initiation, regular service, and proper protocols for invocation and offering.

Grimoire traditions assign planetary and elemental spirits as guardians. Olympic spirits from Renaissance grimoires and the four elemental kings serve protective functions when properly conjured and bound to service through traditional ceremony.

Creating Spirit Sigils

Sigils provide a physical focus for guardian spirit relationships. Traditional methods include receiving the spirit's sigil through vision or automatic drawing, using established sigils from grimoires, or constructing sigils through gematria and sacred geometry.

When creating original sigils, enter trance or visionary state and request the spirit reveal its sign. Draw what you perceive without conscious interference. Alternatively, convert the spirit's name to numbers using Hebrew, Greek, or Latin gematria, then plot these numbers on a magick square corresponding to the spirit's planetary or elemental nature.

Protocol for Established Traditions

When working with guardian spirits from living traditions (Tibetan Buddhism, vodou, santería, Catholic saint veneration), respect existing protocols. Seek proper initiation or empowerment where required. Do not innovate or combine incompatible systems.

Guardian spirits tied to specific cultural and religious contexts carry the full weight of those systems. Attempting to work with Yemaya and Oya simultaneously without understanding their relationship within vodou creates spiritual conflict. Working with conflicting Tibetan dharmapalas without proper empowerment creates dangerous contradictions within Tibetan Buddhist frameworks.

Study the tradition thoroughly or work with qualified initiates. Guardian spirits from closed practices require proper entry into those systems.

Maintaining Guardian Relationships

Guardian spirits require ongoing relationship maintenance. Regular offerings appropriate to the spirit's nature, periodic invocations acknowledging their presence and protection, and honoring commitments made during initial contact sustain the relationship.

Neglecting a guardian spirit after establishing the relationship creates problems. The spirit may withdraw protection, demand renewed attention through disruptive manifestations, or sever the connection entirely. Consistency matters more than elaborate ceremony.

Artificial Spirits

Apart from spirits and intelligences attracted through conjuration or offering, practitioners can create artificial spirits. An artificial spirit is made from energy shaped and programmed by the practitioner, similar to an artificial intelligence program. These entities are created for long and short-term use and are known by many names across traditions.

Terminology Across Traditions

In traditional European witchcraft, artificials are sometimes known as a fetch or bud-will. In ceremonial magick they are often called egregores, or when constructed from one or more of the four elements, artificial elementals. Chaos magick practitioners generally call them servitors. Tibetan Buddhism uses the term tulpa (roughly translating to "Mind Emanation"). The construction and use are more or less the same regardless of terminology.

Historical Examples

The Golem of Prague (1580): Rabbi Loeb created an artificial spirit that inhabited and animated a physical form to protect the Jewish community from false accusations of ritual murder. The golem was given life by writing one of the names of God, EMETH, on its head. The spirit was deactivated by changing EMETH to METH (meaning "dead" in Hebrew) by wiping off the first letter. Stories vary about the golem's ultimate fate, but it was said to be sealed in a secret passage in a synagogue where it remains.

Alexandra David Néel's Tulpa (1920s): The French explorer who traveled Tibet disguised as a beggar and lama described creating an artificial spirit in her book Magic and Mystery in Tibet. She sealed herself in a cave and concentrated on creating a short, good-natured monk. After a few weeks, the tulpa-monk followed her on travels and was seen by other members of her traveling party. Problems arose when the monk began changing outside her control, his appearance shifting from portly and good-natured to gaunt and sinister. She dismantled the spirit only with great effort over several months.

GOTOS of the Fraternitas Saturni: This German magickal order regarded an egregore named GOTOS (acronym for Gradus Ordinis Templi Orientis Saturni) as a secret chief. The egregore was fed into by everyone in the order, creating a group mind that could be called upon to advise the order with the weight of its collected wisdom.

Purpose and Function

Artificial spirits can be made for almost any purpose, though this grimoire focuses primarily on magickal defense and protection. In general, artificial spirits are meant to be temporary and designed to dissipate upon completion of their task or upon a certain date.

Permanent servitors can be constructed but must be carefully looked after and fed with energy to keep them in line, lest they begin to take their nourishment and thus their programming from elsewhere, as with Alexandra David Néel's runaway tulpa.

Design Considerations

Form: The form is limited only by imagination and should in some way indicate the spirit's function. A servitor made to warn of danger could take the shape of a cloud of eyes and ears. A servitor meant to guard a door could take the form of a knight in armor. Be aware that the servitor may take on the characteristics of its form. If you want a servitor to charge into battle, don't make it cute and cuddly. Similarly, if you are concerned about causing harm in your response to danger, do not make it into the form of a bear.

Name: The name should represent its function in some way. You can choose one word and jumble the letters, or pick a combination of words that you condense. The word "protector" could become "Rectoport." The words "binder of harm" can become "Binderham" by removing the word "of" and the repeating letter "r" from harm. An artificial spirit created primarily from an elemental or planetary force can be named with a word that recalls that force. Madim (Hebrew name for Mars) could be used for a servitor made with energy from that planetary sphere.

Sigil: Construct a sigil from traditional methods by combining letters into a symbol where individual letters are not immediately apparent. You can trace a sigil upon kameas or Rose Cross Lamen if you know how. You can also make a chart of your own construction and trace a sigil on it.

Physical Link: Though not strictly necessary, writing the name and sigil on paper forms a magickal link and home for the spirit. This paper can be used to feed the servitor and issue further instructions. The spirit's orders and symbols appropriate to the working can be added, as can oils and powders consistent with the spirit's nature. For long-term spirits, engrave the sigil and name onto a statue or other object that will serve as a powerful guardian.

Defense Against Hostile Artificial Spirits

If you suspect an artificial spirit has been sent against you, several methods of combat exist.

Thought-Form Spirits: Some artificial spirits are nothing more than thought-forms projected by a creator without any other type of energy put into them. In this case you can destroy them by thinking them away. Imagine them being obliterated. From mind they came and by mind they go.

Artificial Elementals: If banishing and visualization fail, you have a stronger problem. Trap the spirit in a triangle (such as the Hekatean spirit trap) and attack it with the opposing element and associated weapons. Alternatively, begin feeding it the element it is made from, making it stronger but infusing it with your will in an attempt to usurp control. This is more dangerous but has advantages. Successfully taking over an artificial spirit creates a powerful magickal link to a potentially unknown attacker.

Usurping Sent Spirits: There are cases where spirits sent to attack someone were usurped by the victim and turned upon the attacker. This is done through making greater offerings to the spirit, binding the spirit as in an exorcism, or appealing to the spirit's nature. In Haiti, a bokor (sorcerer) sent one of the barons (lwa associated with death and graveyards) against another bokor. The targeted sorcerer made prayers to the same baron and left it up to the baron to decide who was justified. In the end, the first bokor who initiated the attack was taken to the grave.

This technique of forcing a spirit to choose between two victims in hopes that the unjustified person will be killed appears in the Pulsa Dinura (Lashes of Fire curse), performed in a cemetery invoking the angel of death, asking him to kill a named victim or kill the person performing the curse. It is up to the angel to decide who deserves death.

Using such techniques is obviously dangerous and advanced work. You will generally be better served by using defensive techniques and methods of reversal and counter-magick rather than attempting to usurp hostile spirits.

Healing Through Nature Spirits

Beyond working with specific deities, guardian spirits, or artificial servitors, the land itself offers powerful healing allies. Trees, rocks, rivers, and other natural places each have their own genii loci, spirits of place that can assist in healing when approached with respect and proper offering.

Building Relationship Through Offering

If you have been making regular offerings to the natural world as part of your practice, you have already begun building relationships with these spirits. Even if they have not made themselves known through direct communication or signs, the bond created through consistent offering establishes a foundation of reciprocity.

The spirits of place are not specific entities like named deities or conjured spirits. They are the consciousness of the land itself: the accumulated awareness of an old tree, the presence within a large boulder, the spirit that flows through a river or dwells at the ocean's edge.

The Healing Working

When you need healing after magickal attack or other spiritual harm, these allies can help process and transform what troubles you.

Choosing a Location:

Go to a place in nature where you feel a particularly strong presence. This might be:

  • An old tree that has witnessed decades or centuries
  • A large boulder or rock formation
  • The ocean or a significant body of water
  • A grove or clearing that feels sacred
  • Any natural place where you sense deep presence

The location should feel powerful but not threatening. You are seeking aid, not testing yourself against overwhelming force.

Entering Trance:

Sit or lie down in contact with the earth. Make yourself receptive to the energies of the place. Speak aloud or silently, explaining that you have been hurt and are in need of healing.

Enter trance through whatever method works best for you:

  • Intense drumming (bring a drum or drum on the earth itself)
  • Breath control techniques
  • Self-hypnosis
  • Meditation
  • Any combination of methods

The goal is to shift your consciousness enough to perceive the spiritual dimension of the place.

Accessing the Spiritual Dimension:

Once in trance, attempt to "enter" the spiritual layer of the location. This cannot be explained mechanically. It is a function of the trance state itself and must be discovered through practice.

If trance alone does not provide access, try falling asleep in the location and entering its spiritual dimension through lucid dreaming. This technique works particularly well with trees, where lying against the trunk can facilitate dream communication.

Meeting the Genii:

Within the spiritual dimension of the place, look for the genius loci. These spirits appear differently depending on the location and your own perceptual framework, but they are always at the center of things: the heart of the tree, the core of the stone, the deepest current of the water.

Explain your situation to the genius. Ask if the place can safely absorb your hurt.

Natural places can often take forces that trouble humans and process them without harm, much as soil processes waste into nutrients. What is poison to one being is not poison to all. The genius will indicate whether it can help or whether you should seek healing elsewhere.

Offering Up the Harm:

If the genius agrees to help, offer up what troubles you. Visualize the magickal attack, the spiritual wounds, or the negative energy flowing out of you and into the place. See it absorbed by the tree, the stone, or the water.

Thank the genius for its aid. Express genuine gratitude for the healing work.

Returning to Regular Consciousness:

When the working feels complete, return to normal awareness. The transition should be gentle; take time to reorient yourself.

Make a physical offering to the place as thanks. This could be:

  • Water poured at the base of a tree
  • Honey or milk
  • Flowers or herbs
  • Tobacco or other traditional offerings
  • A formal offering ceremony as taught in your tradition

The offering completes the exchange and honors the relationship you have built.

Important Considerations

Respect Boundaries: If a genius indicates it cannot or will not help, accept this answer. Not every place is suited for every type of healing work.

Reciprocity Matters: Regular offerings before you need help establish the relationship that makes this healing possible. Coming only when you need something, without prior relationship, is less likely to succeed.

Physical Safety: Choose locations where you can safely enter trance or sleep. Avoid dangerous terrain, extreme weather, or places where you might be disturbed by others.

Integration: After the healing, continue your regular offerings to the place. The relationship should be ongoing, not transactional.

Working with the Saints

A practical guide to establishing relationships with saints, requesting their assistance, and honoring them through veneration.

The Sacred Nature of Saints

Saints fulfill the needs of devotees and protect from harm. They bless endeavors and intervene in lives. Above all else, saints are sacred beings. This cannot be stressed enough. Standing in a saint's presence means standing in the presence of the holy, regardless of whether that saint lived a particularly holy life while breathing.

This point gets lost easily when focusing on which saint handles which practical concern. When considering how certain saints assist with love matters, travel protection, or locating lost objects, it bears remembering that these are beings worthy of reverence, not personal assistants or magickal vending machines. The saint's mere presence constitutes a gift and blessing. Saints need not perform any service for the relationship to hold profound meaning. Beyond material assistance, saints teach lessons about love, bravery, generosity, and selflessness. The miracles are a bonus, not the primary purpose.

Approaching Saints Based on Your Needs

Your approach depends entirely on what you seek. Perhaps you want nothing at all. Maybe you've discovered a saint you admire or one designated as your patron, the saint meant to serve as your spiritual guardian. Lighting a candle on their feast day as a simple gesture of respect might be entirely sufficient and deeply fulfilling. Wearing a medallion or carrying a prayer card because it brings peace of mind may be all you need. Without requiring concrete assistance, simply enjoying a saint's company is enough.

However, when facing genuine difficulty and needing sacred intervention, saints deliver miracles. This defines them. Three questions arise:

  • How do I ask for a miracle?
  • How will I know my request reached them?
  • Which saint should I approach?

Understanding Veneration

Every tradition acknowledging saints provides approved methods for contact and veneration. Veneration is central here. Saints receive veneration, not worship. That distinction matters. The word comes from Latin veneratus and means:

  1. Regarding someone with reverential respect or admiring deference
  2. Honoring through ritual acts of devotion

Despite sounding formal, veneration is anything but rigid. The word connects to Venus, the Roman goddess of love. At its root, veneration relates to love itself. Beloved saints, the renowned miracle workers, are genuinely loved. Ideally, you will find saints you love who love you in return.

The simplest path to relationship with a saint is through heartfelt veneration, the love within you. Everything else is secondary. Traditional techniques exist for communication and requesting help, but speaking your pain, needs, and deepest feelings directly to a saint works just as well. Words spoken aloud or silently in your heart carry equal weight. Though rituals and spells accompany some saints, all have historically responded to sincere cries from the heart.

Location and Communication

Many journey to pilgrimage sites linked to specific saints, believing pleas carry more weight from certain locations. Better reception may occur at these places, but location poses no barrier. Petitions have been delivered from everywhere.

A statue is not the saint. Statues serve as representations only. Saints are not lifeless objects or human creations. They are vital, responsive sacred beings. They exist beyond imagination or archetype. You speak to them, not at them, and they potentially hear and respond. Admiring a saint from distance differs from veneration, which involves genuine relationship. Healthy relationships flow both ways.

The Reciprocal Relationship

What do saints gain from this arrangement? Many saints vowed to provide help, creating a spiritual component beyond any gift devotees can offer. Still, these relationships remain reciprocal. Devotees provide veneration; saints provide assistance. Either party may initiate contact. Saints sometimes appear in dreams or visions to offer their patronage voluntarily.

Methods of Veneration

Gestures of veneration represent the simplest way to begin a relationship. The most basic and traditional gesture involves lighting candles, oil lamps, or incense. This can happen at shrines, though home altars serve most devotees worldwide. Individual saints may have specific associated rituals. Popular saints often have annual public festivals.

Tradition-Specific Practices

Roman Catholic: Saints may be petitioned or thanked through novenas, nine-day prayer rituals.

Orthodox: Saints are traditionally venerated through sacred images called icons.

Jewish: Saints are venerated at gravesites through psalm recitation or written notes detailing needs and desires, placed directly on the grave or tucked into cracks in the stone.

The Stone Ritual

Saints are not always available. They may be performing miracles elsewhere, visiting celestial realms, or communing with other saints. Leaving a stone on a saint's tomb serves as leaving a message. See The Stone Ritual for the full ritual.

Veneration remains fluid. Cultures and traditions borrow and adapt from each other. Many saints transcend denominational boundaries. If a practice resonates with you, use it or modify it to suit your spiritual needs.

La Promesa: Requesting Miracles

When desperation strikes and you truly need a miracle, the most traditional and effective method is La Promesa ("the promise"). This ancient approach exists across virtually all spiritual traditions with variations. Saints have been venerated this way for thousands of years. See La Promesa for the full ritual.

Saints and Magick

Less conventional approaches exist. Many saints are invoked through magick spells, though this remains controversial and rarely receives official approval. Ironically, saints most associated with magick (the so-called "magickal saints") rank among the oldest, most venerated, and officially recognized. These saints participate in workings they likely would have condemned while alive, at least according to their recorded histories. Perhaps they reconsidered after death. Or perhaps they provide acceptable facades allowing devotees continued access to older spiritual practices.

Not all saints connect with magick. Where applicable, spells appear in individual saint entries.

Spells Versus Prayers

Spells and prayers are closely related, but prayers request while spells demand.

Principles for Working Magick with Saints

Coincidences as Communication: Magickal philosophy holds that coincidences don't exist. They are signs requiring attention. Not all carry equal significance, but all deserve consideration. Saints communicate through apparent coincidences. If you petition a saint in the morning and receive an unexpected image of their symbol by afternoon, don't dismiss it. This may be direct confirmation that your request arrived. Pay attention. More messages may follow. Ignoring coincidences equals discarding unopened mail.

The Core of Every Spell: Many casting styles exist, but every spell's crucial component is its goal. You must want the outcome wholeheartedly, truly, and deeply.

Anyone Can Cast: Experience helps but isn't required. Beginners have luck. Not every spell succeeds, even for the experienced, though they recognize failure faster and adjust. You need not hire professionals. Self-cast spells carry the most power because no one wants your goals more than you do. Spell-casting is a learnable skill. Natural talent varies, but anyone can develop ability through effort.

Emotional Fuel: Focus intensely on your desire while casting. Fear, longing, and passionate emotion activate your spell.

Visualization: During casting, see your goal as already achieved. Seeking health? Visualize yourself vital and pain-free. Seeking fertility? Picture yourself holding a baby. This step is necessary even when painful or when hope feels distant. Force yourself to envision the best outcome.

Present Tense: Spells and affirmations are spoken as if already true. Say "My illness is healed" rather than "My illness will be healed." Future tense keeps goals perpetually out of reach.

Magick Complements Action: Spells supplement practical effort. They don't replace it. Petitioning for employment still requires showing up for interviews. Magick doesn't substitute for medical care. In emergencies, invoke spiritual help and call emergency services.

Working Together

Those who actively venerate saints often speak of "working with" them. Saint and devotee collaborate to solve seemingly impossible situations. The devotee is not a passive recipient. Saint veneration, and spellwork generally, does not encourage passivity. It enables the living to shape their own destiny in partnership with the sacred dead.

When Things Don't Work

Spells are not recipes with guaranteed outcomes. They are unpredictable by nature. Otherwise they would be science experiments, not magick. Sometimes they exceed expectations. Sometimes they work differently than anticipated. Sometimes they fail entirely. The same applies to miracles. If miracles were predictable, they would cease to be miraculous.

Saints sometimes don't answer. Occasionally they explain why through dreams or communication. Often the reason remains mysterious, perhaps revealed only when you can confront them directly in the afterlife.

Possible Explanations for Failure

  • Wrong spell for your situation
  • Spell cast incorrectly (try again, especially if you struggled to focus or lacked privacy)
  • Something angered the saint
  • You requested something you believe is best, but the saint knows otherwise

Many practitioners later feel relieved when desired outcomes didn't materialize. What seemed desperately wanted proved not to serve our true interests. Saints sometimes know something better awaits, something your current request would prevent. You might pray to preserve a relationship while the saint knows a better partner comes after it ends.

Spiritual growth sometimes requires pain we would choose to avoid. Or perhaps the saint simply hasn't received your appeal yet. Or you approached the wrong saint entirely, the spiritual equivalent of knocking on the wrong door. No harm comes from this, but you may be ignored.

Spells, rituals, and appeals succeed most reliably when working with saints who are right for you: your personal allies and guardians.

Finding Your Saints

Thousands of saints exist. How do you find the right one for you? Fortunately, various techniques can help identify your personal saints.

The simplest method is to explore descriptions of different saints. Pay attention to which ones resonate most deeply. Whose story touched you profoundly? If you find yourself spontaneously thinking of a saint late at night or cannot get a story out of your mind, this may indicate a personal connection.

Some people devote themselves to only one saint. Others maintain relationships with an entire pantheon. Each individual's needs are different.

Patronages

Saints possess "patronages," meaning that something or someone is under their charge and care. Saints are affiliated with professions, hobbies, ethnicities, locations, and virtually everything imaginable. If you are a mime, for instance, Saint Julian the Hospitaller is your professional patron and may be appealed to for help.

Some saints patronize illnesses and conditions. Those suffering from Parkinson's disease might appeal to Pope John Paul II. Saints who specialize in specific crises or disasters may assist in those situations even if they are not otherwise your primary saint. If a dangerous storm approaches, you can invoke Saint Barbara even if she is not technically your matron saint.

Saints Across Traditions

Although this upsets some devotees, many (if not most) saints perform miracles for those outside their original spiritual tradition. In death, many saints are far more tolerant than they ever were while alive. In North Africa, Muslims and Jews traditionally invoke each other's saints. The most famous wonder-working saints, like Rita or Anthony of Padua, perform miracles for all. Saints from spiritual traditions not your own may still assist you. Never assume they will not, particularly if other signs indicate some sort of bond.

Clues to Your Personal Patrons

Shared Name: Many traditions consider that sharing a name creates an unbreakable bond. A saint whose name you share may be obligated to serve as your patron. This is one reason why so many name their children after powerful saints.

Birth Date: Were you born on a day associated with a saint? This may indicate patronage. If 17 January is your birthday, then Roseline of Villeneuve, who celebrates her feast on that day, may be your saint.

Birth Location: If you were born in a location or hospital named after a saint, you may be able to claim that saint's patronage as well.

Bibliomancy Ritual

Bibliomancy is the art of divination using a book as a tool, just as cartomancy utilizes cards. This technique can help identify your saintly spiritual guardian. See Bibliomancy for Patron Saints for the full ritual.

Fra Geremia's Healing Ritual

A different ritual brought the 16th-century healer and Franciscan friar Geremia Da Udine local celebrity (and also an invitation to speak with the Inquisition). His method was intended to provide healing and identify an ailing person's patron saint simultaneously. It remains viable today. See Fra Geremia's Healing Ritual for the full ritual.

Spirits in Spell-casting

Across every culture and era, practitioners have sought the participation of powerful spirits in their magickal work. This guide explores the principles, dynamics, and ethics of spirit-oriented spell-casting, a practice that stands apart from other methods of magick.

What is Spirit-oriented Spell-casting?

In most forms of spell-casting, the practitioner performs the entire working from beginning to end. Spirit-oriented spells operate differently. The practitioner's role is to induce, persuade, or negotiate with a powerful spirit, typically one who specializes in a particular domain, to perform the magickal action on the practitioner's behalf. The spell itself becomes the vehicle for securing that cooperation.

This approach sits close to the boundary between magick and religion, and in some cases the two cannot be fully separated. Many magickal practices preserve what were once formal, widespread religious traditions. Spirits honored as gods and goddesses in religious contexts appear throughout magickal workings, but magick draws a key distinction: religion may involve devotion and worship, while magick seeks a reciprocal, cooperative relationship. Both spirit and human are understood to have needs, and a successful spell fulfills them mutually.

Why Spirits Participate

Spirits assist practitioners for a range of reasons. Some are broadly benevolent. Others may hold specific affection for an individual. The most fundamental answer, however, is that it falls within their nature and domain to do so. Just as a healer treats illness, each spirit operates within a sphere of expertise. This is why petitioning the correct spirit for a given purpose matters, though the spirits who work most consistently and powerfully are always personal guardians, allies, and ancestral spirits.

There are spirits attached to every conceivable topic, extending well beyond the commonly known categories of love, protection, and healing. If a domain or concept exists, at least one spirit is associated with it.

The Spectrum of Spirits

One person's guardian angel may be another's demon. First Corinthians 10:20 describes pagan sacrifices as offerings made to demons, though the pagans themselves would have strongly disagreed. Many spirits invoked in magick seem obscure today, but they were once prominent figures in the spiritual landscape. The rise of Christianity and Islam pushed many renowned spirits to the margins, but this does not diminish their potential power.

Other spirits, depending on the tradition, are more vital and empowered now than ever before. Any spirit believed to have the power to assist should be treated with respect and consideration. Never underestimate even a seemingly minor spiritual entity.

The Principle of Reciprocity

At its best, the human-spirit alliance creates relationships of deep affection, love, and devotion. A barter dynamic underlies the exchange: practitioners feed the spirits, the spirits care for the practitioners, and the cycle strengthens over time. The single most important principle in this work is reciprocity.

When making a request, present an offering. When the request is fulfilled, respond with acknowledgment, whether through prayer, gesture, or a gift. Spirits, like people, have preferences. Thousands of years of accumulated wisdom inform these practices, so there is no need to figure everything out alone, though intuition may itself be divinely inspired.

Inner and Outer Power

Spirit-partnership magick is widely considered one of the most potent forms of practice. It operates on the principle that magick involves a partnership between inner powers (those that are part of the practitioner) and outer powers (those that exist independently). Neither is sufficient alone. Physical materials anchor intention, while spiritual allies provide force and direction beyond what the practitioner can generate independently.

Alternative Approaches

Spirit-oriented spell-casting is not required for effective magickal practice. Many systems, including Hoodoo, operate as practical magick without requiring direct spiritual encounters. Practitioners who prefer not to engage with spirits can focus on material-based or energy-based methods instead. Those who do maintain a relationship with specific spirits may incorporate spiritual petition into virtually any spell they cast.

Lunar Deities

To our earliest ancestors, the moon was a god. The moon defined the passage of time as it changed phases throughout the lunar month, lighting the nighttime sky and then disappearing. Despite the shift from lunar- to solar-dominant worship with the start of more permanent settlements, many moon deities are still honored and worshipped to this day. While many associate the moon with the perception of feminine energy, moon deities have appeared across the gender spectrum throughout human history and in some cases, individual moon gods have changed gender over time.

The variations on mythology surrounding the moon are truly endless. Some ancient cultures adapted and adopted moon deities from other societies, while others worshipped different deities for varying aspects of the moon. Some moon gods were considered personifications of the moon itself, others were deities of the moon, and still more were simply associated with it.

Below you will find descriptions of some of the lunar deities commonly referenced in modern witchcraft. The full list of moon deities one can connect with is far longer, exemplifying the endless potential of the moon's power.

Lunar Deities in the Entity Grimoire

  • Arianrhode: Celtic/Welsh, silver wheel goddess of naming and fate
  • Artemis: Greek, mistress of wild nature, moon goddess and twin of Apollo
  • Chang'O: Chinese, lunar goddess who ascended to the moon
  • Chandra: Hindu, deity of the moon and timekeeping
  • Coyolxauhqui: Aztec, moon goddess whose severed head rolls through the sky
  • Kwan Yin: East Asian, bodhisattva of compassion often depicted with moon
  • Luna: Roman, spirit of the moon
  • Mama Quilla: Incan, Mother Moon, defender of women and marriage
  • Mani: Norse, personification of the moon
  • Nanna: Sumerian/Mesopotamian, ancient moon god and keeper of time
  • Selene: Greek, ancient moon goddess and matron of magickians
  • Hekate: Greek, goddess of witchcraft and the dark/waning moon

The Triple Goddess

Trinities have long been considered sacred across cultures and traditions. Many deities embody divine triplicity: the Tridevi, the Morrígan, the three Fates, and the Christian trinity among them. The Triple Goddess as understood in modern Neopaganism and Wicca is not a single deity but an archetype: a symbolic framework associated with the moon's phases and the many expressions of feminine divine power.

The Triple Goddess is represented by the triple moon symbol, a full moon flanked by two crescents, and is broadly associated with the waxing, full, and waning or dark moon. Some practitioners associate the archetype with the trio of Artemis, Selene, and Hekate.

For a time, the three phases were mapped onto perceived stages of a woman's life: maiden (waxing), mother (full), and crone (waning/dark). Many modern witches have found these labels limiting. The archetype can hold much more:

  • The underworld, the earth, and the heavens
  • The three selves: id, ego, and superego
  • The three souls of witchcraft
  • The three phases of life: youth, adulthood, and old age

The meaning you bring to it is the meaning it holds. Choose whichever representation resonates.

⚠️
A note on Hekate: Hekate is called a triple goddess because of her dominion over the sky, land, and underworld, not because she represents the maiden/mother/crone framework. Her triple nature is one of cosmic realm and liminal power, not a life-stage archetype. See her page for full context.
