Source Notes

Origin and Period

Apollo is a god of hunting and healing of the Greek tradition, possibly with roots in cultures of Asia Minor. His known period of worship spans circa 1300 BC and earlier until Christianization circa 400 AD and probably later.

Synonyms

Apellon (pre-Homeric); Atepomarus (Celtic).

Centers of Cult

Delos, Pylo-Delphi, and many other sanctuaries throughout the Greek world.

Art References

The Parthenon frieze; the Belvedere Apollo triumphing over the Python; Apollo and Daphne; a famed but lost statue from Delos; Apollo holding the three Graces in his right hand; other contemporary sculpture and painting.

Literary Sources

The Iliad and Odyssey (Homer); the Theogony and Hymn to Apollo (Hesiod); and various other temple hymns.

Character and Lineage

One of the major Greek deities, Apollo was always perceived as a god who epitomizes youthful masculinity, possibly with early links to Lycia in Asia Minor (Hittite) and to Minoan Crete. He is generally a distant rather than an intimate and approachable god. His mother is Leto, who wandered the world in great suffering until she chanced on the island of Delos where she found refuge. Apollo is often portrayed as part of a triad with Leto and Artemis. He epitomizes the transition between adolescence and manhood in Greek male society.

Sanctuaries

At Delphi his sanctuary is central to the complex. At Delos it appears secondary to that of Artemis.

Healing and Pestilence

The paean dance of healing, particularly known from the Hyakinthia festival at Amyklai (Sparta), is closely identified with the Apollo cult. He is a god of healing but also of pestilence. He is the father of Asklepios, the god of healing, and he is continually associated with purification rites and oracles.

Hunter and Lyre Player

Generally Apollo is drawn as a god of hunters carrying a bow and arrow and associated with a stag or roe. He is also pictured with lions. He became, improbably, the patron god of poets and leader of the Muses, daughters of Zeus. Literature often presents Apollo in a dual aspect of fearsome hunter and gracious player of the lyre.

Acts of Mercilessness and Banishment

In his fearsome aspect he was at times merciless, killing the many children of Niobe, who had boasted of them to the chagrin of Leto. He fought and slew the Delphic python and the Olympic Cyclopes, but in both cases himself became subject to general laws of morality and suffered temporary banishment.

Mystical Number

Apollo is strongly associated with the mystical number seven, almost certainly a Mesopotamian concept.

Ugaritic and Celtic Identifications

In Ugaritic inscriptions he is referred to as Resep of the Arrow (see Resep). Apollo was widely revered under various local synonyms by the Celts.

Rampion as Funereal Offering

The ancient Greeks treated rampion (Campanula rapunculus) as a funereal vegetable and laid it on golden plates as an offering to Apollo. Its humble field-and-garden character did not keep it from a place at his altar.

Source Notes

Origin and Period

Ares is the Greek god of war. The name has been interpreted as throng of war. His known period of worship runs from circa 800 BC, but probably from earlier times, until Christianization circa 400 AD. No synonyms are recorded.

Centers of Cult

No sanctuaries are known until Roman times, when a temple was dedicated in the Agora in Athens.

Art References

He appears on the Parthenon frieze, in a celebrated statue by Alkamenes, and in other contemporary sculpture.

Literary Sources

Chiefly the Iliad of Homer and the Theogony of Hesiod.

Character and Lineage

Ares is a lesser known member of the Olympic pantheon of great gods, the son of Zeus and Hera, who allegedly lived in Thrace. As a warrior god he is contrasted with the more prominent and successful goddess Athena, who fought and vanquished him in a war between the gods. While Athena stands for victory in battle through glory and honor, Ares epitomizes the evil and more brutal aspects of warfare. In the eyes of Zeus he is the most hateful of gods. His war chariot is pulled by Phobos (fear) and Deimos (terror).

Sons of Ares

Ares' sons were even more barbaric than he. Kyknos was a ferocious killer who, until slain by Herakles, was proposing a temple constructed of human skulls. Another notorious son of Ares was the dragon slain by Kadmos as he sought to found the city of Thebes. Its teeth, which Kadmos sowed in the earth, germinated and sprang up as warriors, the grandsons of Ares, who promptly turned on each other in mortal combat.

Liaison with Aphrodite

Ares entered into a brief liaison with Aphrodite, the goddess consort of Hephaistos, and through her fathered a daughter, Harmonia, whom Kadmos later married, thus paving the way to establish Thebes in an atmosphere of peace and harmony.

Shrine to Artemis

Artemis is depicted as a young goddess wearing a horned or lunar headdress, carrying a crescent-shaped bow and arrows, and accompanied by a stag or a pack of hunting dogs. She is the moon goddess and twin counterpart to Apollo, god of the sun. Born to Leto and Zeus, she arrived first and immediately helped midwife her twin brother into the world, in this aspect she is sometimes called Cynthia, linking the moon to women and the act of birth. Artemis is a chaste goddess beholden to only herself. Her mythology holds a message for moon magick practitioners: working in tune with nature, within and without, and dedicating oneself to mastery, can lead like her arrows to hitting any target.

Ancient mistress of wild nature, witchcraft, women's mysteries. Regulates fertility of humans/animals/plants. Guardian of thresholds, hunts, sacred groves. Bear origins, Lady of Beasts. Twin to Apollo, born first, midwifed his birth. Colors white/silver.

Diana: Italian Forest Queen

Indigenous Italian (possibly Etruscan) deity with stronger night/darkness/magick associations than Artemis. Lives in Forest of Nemi with consort Virbius, horned stag spirit subordinate to her.

Goddess-Consort Pattern

Diana and Virbius exemplify original Pagan hierarchy: powerful goddess with male consort whom she initiates and tutors. Goddess is eternal and dominant.

Christian Inversion: Made male devil dominant over female witches, inverting original power structure where goddess ruled.

Devil's Grandmother: Russian/Central/Northern European folklore preserves memory. She taught devil everything, retained secrets, knows tricks he doesn't, legend both diabolized old women and recalled when women's wisdom was respected.

Celtic Worship & Persecution

Worshipped as log in Celtic Europe. Male wolf-shamans/lunar priests served her. Early Christians saw cult as major rival. When Christianity gained power, Diana vilified as Queen of Witches and Satan's bride. A Spanish Inquisitor declared, "Diana is the devil."

Despite 6th-10th century persecution, worship continued. Inquisition called witchcraft "The Society of Diana." Central to contemporary Stregheria.

Midwife Goddess of Life and Death

Artemis is the sacred Greek midwife whose first act upon being born was to help her mother Leto give birth to her twin brother Apollo. This primordial midwife experience established her eternal role as protector of childbirth and midwifery.

Artemis held the ultimate power over birthing outcomes: she was the Greek deity responsible for determining which women died in childbirth and which survived. This divine authority over the threshold between life and death during birth made her both revered and feared by pregnant women and midwives throughout the ancient Greek world.

Midwives in ancient times were affiliated with shrines and temples in Egypt, Sumeria, and elsewhere in Asia and Africa as well as among the Aztecs and Incas. Birth was considered sacred and magickal but also a dangerous experience requiring divine protection.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household, offerings to Artemis include cedar, deer tokens, jasmine, myrtle, white blooms, and frankincense (manna) incense. The bow with its arrows and the torch She carries serve as Her tokens. The colour linked to Her is green. Her sacred animals include the deer, the dog, the bear, the partridge, and the quail. Plants sacred to Her include amaranthus, palm, the cypress, peanut, and wormwood.

Shrine to Artemis

Notes

Principally a goddess of animals and hunting, but in Greek-speaking Asia she is a mother goddess. Her known period of worship runs from circa 800 BCE and earlier until Christianization around 400 CE, and probably later. Her synonym Potnia Theron means mistress of the animals. Centers of cult included Antioch-near-Pisidia, Delos, Magnesia-on-the-Maeander, Pamphylia, Perge, and Ephesus in Turkey. Cultic statues survive, most notably the multibreasted figures at Ephesus, and her literary sources include cuneiform texts modeled on earlier Asian forms, the Iliad, and the Theogony.

Artemis is a deity of very ancient origins who survived and attracted great popularity in both Asia Minor and Greece into Christian times, when much of her ethos was arguably transferred to the Virgin Mary. Both figures enjoyed major sanctuaries at Ephesus. As an Asiatic goddess she was often drawn winged and standing between wild animals, equipped with boots, a torch, and a pointed cap. She is also a strongly androgynous figure, a feature depicted dramatically in the statue of Artemis of Ephesus. Her temple at Ephesus dates from the fourth century BCE and ranks among the seven wonders of the world. The cult statues were carried in procession on May 25 among a congregation of up to thirty thousand.

To the Greeks she is the daughter of Zeus and Leto, and she was honored in the sanctuary on Delos with its celebrated Horn Altar from circa 700 BCE. In Greek mythology the androgynous aspect was firmly discounted. In her earliest pre-Homeric form the Mistress of Animals suckles the young of every wild creature that roams the fields. As a huntress she uses a bow and arrows. By Homeric times the ferocity of this prehistoric element has waned in favor of a more timid image of a young girl dominated robustly by her stepmother Hera. A contrary character study in the Odyssey pictures her more positively as a virgin goddess chasing and killing boars and hinds over the hills and fields, fleet of foot and in company with a band of nymphs. She presides over nature and over the initiation rituals of young girls. She is also a goddess of blood sacrifice. A cruel element emerged as she threatened any maiden who turned to the role of wife. Paradoxically, and more in keeping with the old Semitic personality, she is also the goddess of birth.

The Artemisia Family

The artemisia botanical family is named in honor of Artemis, who rules magick, fertility, psychic gifts, and wild female nature. Her favorite plants share her nature: they bear profound gifts but are prickly, volatile, and potentially dangerous, and few plants are more closely tied to the magickal arts. The two most famous members of the family are Mugwort and Wormwood.

Dionysus (Bacchus or Liber to the Romans) is the god of wine, ecstasy, theater, liberation, and divine madness. Born from Zeus's thigh after his mother Semele was destroyed, Dionysus represents the breakdown of boundaries between human and divine, male and female, civilization and wilderness. He is a god of extremes who brings both euphoric joy and terrifying madness. His worship involved ecstatic rites, theatrical performances, and the dissolution of normal social constraints. He liberates his devotees from oppression and rigidity but also brings chaos to those who resist him.

Ritual Uses

Invoke Dionysus for liberation from oppression, addiction recovery (paradoxically, as god of wine), creative inspiration, theatrical pursuits, ecstatic spiritual experiences, and sexual healing. Work with him to break free from rigid constraints and embrace transformation. His mysteries involve death and rebirth symbolism. He is powerful for fertility magick and connecting with wild nature. Approach him through wine rituals, music, dance, and theater.

Offerings

Wine (lots of wine), ivy and grape vines, pine cones, masks, fritelle (Roman offering: flour, cheese, eggs, apple, lemon), honey, fruit, theatrical performances in his honor, ecstatic dancing, simple libations.

Favored People

Women (especially his devoted Maenads), actors and dancers, mystics, devotees of ecstatic rites, those oppressed by rigid social structures, vintners and wine makers, theater practitioners, those seeking liberation and transformation, those seeking freedom.

Petition For

Liberation from oppression or madness, joy and ecstatic experience, sexual healing and freedom, creativity and inspiration in performance arts, success in theater and wine-making, fertility, healing of addiction, transformation through dissolution of boundaries, connection to wild nature, wine blessings, freedom.

Warnings

To resist Dionysus is to risk madness. His initiatory path may involve temporary or ecstatic disorientation. Ensure consent and community safeguards in ecstatic rites. Never perform self-harming or reckless initiations. Respect boundaries of participants and do not commercialize mystery practices. His power dissolves boundaries and can be dangerous if approached without proper respect and preparation. Observe wine rites responsibly. Never use his name to justify harmful excess. Offer simple wine and gratitude, respect communal limits.

Additional Notes

Dionysus was twice-born: once from his mother Semele and once from Zeus's thigh. He traveled to India and throughout the Mediterranean spreading his cult. His followers included the Maenads (female devotees) who were said to tear apart animals and even people in their ecstatic frenzy. His sacred animals include panthers, bulls, serpents, and donkeys. The thyrsus (pine cone-tipped staff) is his attribute. He is associated with masks, representing transformation and the theatrical. His mysteries at Eleusis and elsewhere involved profound initiatory experiences.

The Green Man and Wilderness Spirit

Dionysus is the Green Man. His images are adorned with grapevines and ivy. Among his epithets is "the night prowler." He is the spirit of untamed wilderness and irrepressible male procreative energy, intoxication, shamanism, magick, joy, madness, and sexual healing.

Ancient Thracian Origins

Dionysus was the last of the twelve deities incorporated into the Olympian pantheon. His original homeland is believed to be Thrace: modern Bulgaria and Romania both claim his birthplace. According to archeologist Marija Gimbutas, Dionysus was the most ancient non-Indo-European god of Old Europe and was initially a botanical spirit.

The Twice-Born God

Dionysus is the twice-born god. He was conceived by Zeus and Persephone, manifested on Earth as the god Zagreus, and then killed. Zeus rescued his heart and served it to Semele, princess of Thebes. Semele became pregnant with Dionysus, but before she could give birth, she died. Zeus removed the unborn Dionysus and placed him within his own thigh, from which he gave birth to Dionysus. Because he was once Persephone's son, Dionysus is sometimes described as Demeter's grandson.

Marriage to Ariadne

Dionysus is the only Olympian god who is not a rapist. Unlike his fellow deities, he is not a seducer of the innocent. He is the only god who consistently honors women. He is the consort of the Cretan goddess Ariadne and her sacred wedding to Dionysus may have been celebrated at May Eve or Midsummer's Eve.

Manifestations and Sacred Forms

Dionysus may manifest in many forms. He may appear as a handsome young man, a bull, or a goat. His phallus has been depicted as huge. In Dionysian processions, participants would carry a statue of Dionysus represented as a huge phallus. He is ritually invoked in the Orphic Hymn to Priapos, the god of gardens and the protector of flocks.

Teacher of the Agricultural Arts

Dionysus taught humanity the art of viniculture, the cultivation of grapes for winemaking. In addition, he taught the people of the Middle East, North Africa, and India agricultural and magickal arts. He is associated with intoxication and ekstasis not only from wine but also from opium, the ritual consumption of the amanita muscaria mushroom, and from the wild orgiastic music and dancing that characterized his cult.

The Maenads and Bacchanals

Dionysus is served by priestesses known as Maenads or Bacchanals. During his cult's festivals, it was believed that spirits known as Thyiades or Mainades possessed the priestesses. The women were allowed to wander from their homes, unaccompanied by male guardians, and participated in rituals involving music, dance, and wine. The worship of Dionysus was so deeply significant to women that it was virtually unstoppable: women who refused to honor the god were driven mad. Because the rites of Dionysus were so sacred to women and dangerous to men who intruded, the Christian Church eventually forced the dances and orgiastic celebrations into the forest.

Allied Spirits and Sacred Companions

Dionysus is allied with Pan, Hecate, Kybele, Demeter, Persephone, and Apollo. Apollo rules Delphi in the summer, but Dionysus rules Delphi in the winter. The two share the altar and each has three months of the year devoted to his worship. The Maenads travel to Mount Parnassus every other year to dance in honor of Dionysus and awaken the sleeping infant god in the sacred liknon, a basket used for winnowing grain.

Christian Demonization of Dionysus

In 1839, German historian Franz Josef Mone (1796–1871) was among the first to link European witchcraft with Pagan religion. Mone was a devout Roman Catholic and not sympathetic to witches. His theory proposed that ancient Germans once lived by the Black Sea among devotees of Dionysus and Hecate.

According to Mone's theory, German slaves eventually fused German and Dionysian traditions into their own religion, characterized by devotion to a horned spirit, nocturnal gatherings, and the practice of magick. When the Germans headed west, slaves and lower classes brought this religion with them. The upper classes perceived it with contempt, eventually distorting Dionysus into the devil.

Dionysus is among those spirits classified as horned gods, though his myth is extensive and he transcends categories. As a shapeshifter, among his favored forms is that of a bull, one of his sacred animals. Dionysus is a close ally of Pan and they are often in each other's company. The satyrs are considered devotees of Dionysus.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household, offerings to Dionysos include ivy, the grape vine, and styrax incense. The thyrsos serves as His emblem. The colour linked to Him is the deep green carried by ivy. His sacred animals include the leopard, the panther, the donkey, and the bull. Plants sacred to Him are the grape, ivy, and pine.

The Roman Cult of Bacchus

Under Roman worship as Bacchus and Liber Pater, his cult flourished from roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE and spread throughout the Roman world. Roman tradition names his parents as Jupiter and Semele, daughter of Kadmos, and holds that Semele was deified only after her death by fire on Olympus. Bacchus grew up in the care of the wet nurse Ino, later known as Leukothea. As a youth he was entrusted to the satyr Silenus.

In Roman iconography Bacchus appears as a youthful figure wearing an ivy or grape crown and carrying a wand or thyrsus, frequently drawn riding in a chariot pulled by leopards. His court includes the female Bacchantes, alongside nymphs, fauns, and satyrs.

His extensive Roman worship commanded a number of festivals, including the Liberalia and the Bacchanalia. These carried strongly phallic connotations, and on some occasions the god was represented ritually by a model phallus.

Magickal Properties

Epona is a great and important Celtic goddess, guardian spirit of horses and their riders. Her name derives from Epos, a Celtic word meaning horse. She is an extremely complex deity who was once widely venerated throughout Europe. Epona is a spirit of abundance and plenty, healing, and death. She is a goddess of peace and the matron of soldiers. Her shrines incorporated therapeutic healing springs. Epona may be a psychopomp, leading souls to the Afterlife. The ancient Celts perceived horses as oracular animals more closely attuned to the will and desires of spirits than human beings. Epona is likely to have been an oracular spirit.

As with virtually all Celtic goddesses, little documentation regarding Epona exists. She was popular throughout virtually the entire ancient Celtic world. Roman soldiers encountered her in Gaul and adored her literally. Uniquely for a Celtic deity, Epona was brought to Rome, enshrined, and assigned her own official feast day, indicating her official recognition as part of the Roman state religion. Epona was especially popular during the first through fourth centuries CE. She was venerated by a wide spectrum of Romano-Celtic society. Epona was beloved by Roman cavalry officers who adopted her as their own guardian goddess.

Ritual Uses

Petition Epona for protection of horses and their riders. Invoke her for abundance, healing, safe passage through difficult terrain, and prosperity. She can be called upon for oracular guidance and as a psychopomp to guide souls safely to the Afterlife.

Offerings

Cakes, fruit, and something for her horses.

Favored People

Horse breeders, horse traders, horse whisperers, horse doctors, equestrians, cavalry.

Petition For

Protection for horses and their riders, abundance, healing, safe passage, prosperity, oracular guidance, and safe passage to the Afterlife.

Warnings

Epona is the matron of soldiers. She has dominion over horses, donkeys, and mules. Those who care for them may consider themselves under Epona's dominion. Those who abuse them should probably avoid attracting Epona's attention.

Additional Notes

Epona is never represented without a horse. A typical image portrays Epona riding side-saddle on a mare. A foal sleeps beneath its mother, suckles from its mother, or eats from a plate that Epona offers. Alternatively Epona is portrayed sitting between several horses that approach her in homage, or she sits between male and female ponies and feeds them. She is occasionally portrayed as a mermaid on horseback. Her attributes include a key, cornucopia, basket of fruit, and the cloth once traditionally used to start horse races. The Mothers are Epona's sometime companions. Sacred animals include horses, dogs, and ravens. Her sacred day is December 18, her Roman feast.

The Uffington Horse

Cut into the chalk hillside at Uffington in south-east England, near an ancient Iron Age hill fort, is the great figure of a white horse visible for miles. It has been proposed that this landmark was made in honour of Epona or her near-equivalent Rhiannon. The two goddesses are so closely aligned in character, symbol, and function that they may in fact be the same deity, known by different names in the Roman and Welsh corners of the Celtic world.

Shrine to Freyja

The Most Beautiful of Norse Spirits

Freya is the most beautiful of the Norse spirits with dominion over love, sex, fertility, magick, witchcraft, death, pleasure, and glory. "Freya" literally means "Lady" and may be a title, not a name. Her twin brother is Freyr or "Lord." She is simultaneously a spirit of fertility and death, beauty and war.

Divine Lineage and Political Position

Freya is the daughter of Njord and Herta (Nerthus), Sea and Earth. She is among the Vanir hostages who joined the Aesir to maintain spiritual peace. Freya, however, is so powerful that she quickly became a dominant force in her new realm.

Witch and Teacher of Magic

Freya is clearly identified as a witch. When she first arrives in Asgard (the Aesir's realm), she teaches the Aesir how to craft charms and potions. It is Freya who introduced Odin to the concept of runes. Völvas and Valkyries serve as her priestesses.

Manifestations and Shape-Shifting

Golden Freya most often manifests as a woman, although she owns a falcon feather cloak that enables her to fly like a falcon and shape-shift as she pleases.

Leader of the Valkyries

Freya leads the Valkyries, the divine choosers of the slain. Under her command they escort fallen warriors to Valhalla's great banqueting halls to feast and prepare for the final battle, Ragnarok. Half of all warriors slain in battle are received into Freya's own hall rather than Odin's.

The Necklace of the Dwarves

Freya was particularly fond of beautiful things. When she discovered four dwarves crafting a magnificent necklace, her desire to possess it was so powerful that she agreed to spend a night with each of them in exchange for it. The necklace became one of her defining attributes. Known by name as Brisingamen, it is the namesake behind the Necklace counted among witches' identifying jewels.

Independent and Autonomous

Most other surviving Norse goddesses are identified as "wives"; Freya is an independent single woman who answers to no one. She was married, but her husband Od mysteriously disappeared. She weeps golden tears for him that transform into amber, but takes her pleasure as she pleases.

Sacred Creatures and Symbols

Two large gray cats, possibly lynxes, named Bee-gold (Honey) and Tree-gold (Amber) pull her chariot. They embody Freya's twin qualities of ferocity and fecundity. She rides a boar into battle (as does her brother Freyr). Her sacred day was Friday; her sacred number 13, the number of months in the lunar calendar. Friday the 13th is thus especially sacred to her, leading to its later malevolent associations under Christianity.

Christian Condemnation and Survival

No spirit annoyed Christian authorities more than Freya. Ironically, the result was that Freya survives more vividly than any other female European spirit. Constant condemnation kept Freya from fading into obscurity.

An insult levied at Freya at the Althing (Parliament) of Iceland initiated the final round of a debate over that country's Christianization: a Christian described Freya as a "bitch goddess."

Queen of Witches

Freya was denounced as a Queen of Witches. Women who venerated her were therefore automatically branded "witches." And of course, Freya's rites and traditions did encourage magickal practice, mediumship, shamanism, and female autonomy, with Freya herself as the role model, behavior the new regime considered abhorrent and sinful.

Widespread Worship

Freya was not an obscure spirit but was beloved and worshipped over a vast European territory including Scandinavia, Iceland, Greenland, the Germanic lands, Holland, and Anglo-Saxon Britain.

Thirteenth-century Icelandic chronicler Snorri Sturluson recorded and preserved many old sagas and poems. He says Freya was the most renowned of all the goddesses, and was still worshipped in his day.

Destruction and Persistence

Freya's last surviving temple, in Magdeburg, Germany, was destroyed by edict of the Emperor Charlemagne. Devotees refused to surrender their faith, however: in 1668, "the worship of Frau Venus" was allegedly still prevalent among the Saxons of Magdeburg.

Mountain Exile and Modern Revival

Freya was banished to the mountain peaks of Norway, Sweden, and Germany to dance with her devotees, especially in The Brocken, the highest peak in the Harz Mountains of central Germany, where she presides over annual Midsummer's and Walpurgis festivities. Freya remains among the most beloved deities among modern Neo-Pagans.

Spinning Goddess and Sacred Plants

Freya is among the spinning goddesses whose sacred plants, flax, hemp, and nettles, were later demonized as "witch plants." These fiber plants, which can be spun into fabric, were once holy to Freya and other goddesses but became suspect after Christianity specifically because of their associations with goddess worship, textile magick, and women's spiritual traditions. The negative associations with hemp, particularly, are believed to derive from its connections to witchcraft, shamanism, and women's magickal traditions rather than from the plant's properties alone. The spinning arts were sacred feminine mysteries, and Freya's association with these plants connects her to the ancient tradition of goddesses who controlled destiny through textile work.

The Mistress

Origin: Greece

Preferred Vocations

  • Queen

Domains & Sacred Objects

  • Marriage
  • Sceptre

Overview

Hera is the Queen of Greece, goddess of women and marriage. In classical Greek myth, she is Zeus' older sister whom he tricked into marriage by taking the form of her sacred bird, a cuckoo caught in a rainstorm. She pitied the little wet, bedraggled bird and held it close to her bosom, at which point the bird transformed back into Zeus.

Their marriage was initially very happy. Their honeymoon night lasted three hundred years: sex was that good. However, sexual fidelity was not in Zeus' vocabulary, and Hera is frequently portrayed as a bitter shrew pursuing Zeus' lovers and punishing them fiercely.

The Deeper Story

Mythologists and archaeologists suggest there's more to this story: Hera was one of the most significant pre-Olympian indigenous Greek goddesses. She is Greece's primordial sacred cow and Great Mother Goddess of matriarchal pre-Hellenic culture.

Original Nature

Hera was initially worshipped as:

  • A Lady of the Beasts
  • A goddess of abundance and fertility
  • An oracular spirit
  • A primordial snake goddess in Argos

In approximately 600 BCE, she made a major transformation. Emphasis was placed on her roles as wife and mother rather than her original functions.

Political Marriage

Dorian invaders married her to Zeus to confer legitimacy on his rule. Many myths emphasize her subjugation by Zeus. Much of what is portrayed as shrewish may be desperate attempts to retain her autonomy and power and to protect her own children's birthright as Zeus' multitudes of other children gained power.

The Rebellion

Hera, together with Poseidon (also an indigenous spirit incorporated into the Olympians), led an unsuccessful rebellion against Zeus. Zeus punished Hera by hanging her from the clouds with anvils tied to her feet. Depressed, Hera wrapped herself in deepest darkness and wandered Earth in the form of a frail, decrepit old woman. She always returns to Zeus.

The Wound: Hera was struck in the right breast by one of Heracles' arrows, inflicting a wound that never heals. She may be the precursor of the image of Our Lady of Sorrows, the beautiful, wounded Madonna.

Name & Renewal

Hera's name may be interpreted as "lady" or as the feminine form of "hero." Alternatively, her name is not Indo-European and has yet to be translated.

Hera seems to have first emerged as a primordial snake goddess in Argos. Each spring, she bathes in the sacred spring of Kanathos near Argos, emerging fresh and youthful like a snake with freshly shed skin. Hera is described as "renewing her virginity." This ritual may be in preparation for performing the Great Rite.

Powers & Invocations

  • She is an oracular spirit
  • She has the power to fulfill virtually any petition
  • She can heal spousal and sexual abuse
  • She punishes by striking those who displease her with sudden madness
  • She may be invoked in cleansing rituals

Attributes & Correspondences

Favored People: Women in general; people born under the zodiac sign Cancer

Manifestation: A radiantly beautiful woman, shining like the sun; however she is also a shape-shifter with many forms. She notoriously disguises herself as a humble, old beggar woman but still expects to be treated like a queen. Woe to those who fail to treat even the humblest with respect. Hera has a fast temper and is quick to administer justice.

Iconography: Depicted wearing a diadem and veil

Attribute: Pomegranate

Colors: Yellow, gold

Birds: Cuckoo, dove, peacock, carrion-crow

Animals: Cow, snake, dragon, crab, snail, and other shelled creatures

Mount: Peacocks pull Hera's chariot

Plants: Vitex agnus-castus, lilies, poppies

Sacred Sites

  • Her sanctuary at Argos (7th century BCE temple built over an earlier shrine), among the oldest Greek temples
  • Her temple at Olympia was older than Zeus' and always distinct
  • Ancient Greek altars were originally open to the air: Hera's temples may have been the first to be roofed

Offerings: Honey, flowers, incense, perfume, pomegranates

Related Entities

Amphitrite, Apollo, Artemis, Asteria, Callisto, Dakini, Dione, Dionysus, Dioscuri, Europa, Ezili Freda Dahomey, Ganymede, Hebe, Hekate, Helen of Troy, Hephaestus, Heracles, Hermes, Hesperides, Horai, Hybla, Hydra, Io, Iris, Kedalion, Ladon, Lady of the Beasts, Leto, Maia, Olympian Spirits, Poseidon, Prometheus, Scylla, Semele, Siren, Themis, Typhon, Zeus

Juno Caprotina: The Horned Manifestation

Among the many paths or manifestations of Hera in her Roman form as Juno is Juno Caprotina. This aspect represents a specific connection to goats and the protection of enslaved and marginalized women.

Juno Caprotina dresses in goatskins and drives a chariot pulled by goats, connecting her to the horned animal imagery associated with fertility, wildness, and primal female power. Her association with goats links her to other horned deities and the sacred power of these animals.

Enslaved women made up a large proportion of her devotees in this manifestation, making Juno Caprotina a goddess who protected and empowered those at the bottom of Roman social hierarchy. She offered hope, protection, and spiritual solace to women who had few other resources.

The name "Caprotina" derives from capra, Latin for "goat," emphasizing her deep connection to these horned animals. Her chariot drawn by goats is a distinctive feature that sets this manifestation apart from other paths of Juno/Hera.

Juno Caprotina's worship is connected to the Lupercalia festival, linking her to Faunus and the fertility rites celebrated in February. Her goat associations connect her to the broader network of horned deities and their life-giving, generative power.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household economy of offerings, Hera receives lilies, peacock feathers, the pomegranate, and a range of fragrant incenses. Her tokens are the crown and the sceptre. Her colour is light blue. The peacock and the cuckoo stand among Her sacred animals, and the pomegranate and the lily among Her sacred plants and fruits.

Shrine to Hermes

Origin: Greece

Preferred Places

  • Boundaries
  • Crossroads
  • Marketplace

Preferred Vocations

  • Magician
  • Merchant
  • Messenger
  • Shepherd
  • Thief
  • Traveler

Domains & Sacred Objects

  • Divination
  • Kadukeus
  • Luck
  • Magick
  • Phallos
  • Stones

Overview

Before Hermes was the winged messenger of Mount Olympus, he was a virile, rustic, pastoral spirit, presiding over the fertility of women and livestock. Hermes was among the best-loved of all Olympian spirits. He is the lord of:

  • Animal husbandry
  • Language, communication, trade, travel
  • Divination (especially cleromancy)

Domains & Powers

Lord of the Crossroads

Hermes' specialty is cleromancy, originally divination using small pebbles, which eventually evolved into dice. He is the trickster lord of the crossroads, spirit of luck and patron of gamblers, especially those who play with dice.

Protection: Hermes protects thieves and also protects against them. He may be invoked for:

  • The gift of gab
  • Business success
  • True omens
  • Mother-wit and cunning

Psychopomp & Shaman

Hermes is a shaman: he travels between realms, hence his eventual role as Zeus' messenger. He is a psychopomp who conveys the souls of the dead to Hades. Sacrifices were made to Hermes on the final day of Greek festivals of the dead to ensure that he would escort the dead souls back to Hades.

If a ghost refuses to vacate your premises, Hermes may be asked to escort them to a more appropriate place. Just be careful: Hermes is not violent or particularly aggressive, but he does enjoy playing tricks and the periodic practical joke. He will be a troublesome spirit for those lacking humor and humility.

The Killer of Argus

Hermes killed Hera's guardian Argus by boring him to death. After he had put him to sleep, Hermes touched the guard with his staff to kill him. He is sometimes considered the patron of euthanasia: the gentle death.

Dream Bringer

Hermes prowls around at night, bringing dreams. You can request that he deliver prophetic dreams or that he provide relief from nightmares.

Birth & Family

Hermes was born in a cave to the goddess Maia; Zeus is his father. He makes his home in Mekone, "Poppy town." Hermes is associated with birth, death, and sex. Although now often portrayed as androgynous, Hermes was originally a very virile phallic deity. His sexual partners include Aphrodite and countless Nymphs. The Greek-born Italian goddess Carmenta may be his official wife.

Inventions

Hermes is credited with many inventions:

  • The musical scale
  • The alphabet
  • Boxing and gymnastics
  • Weights and measures
  • Olive culture (Athena may have brought the olive tree, but Hermes taught people how to process the fruit and oil)
  • The lyre: fashioned from the shell of a tortoise and the gut of a sacrificed bull
  • The flute: which he later traded to Apollo in exchange for instruction in magick and a golden caduceus

Worship & Correspondences

Favored People: Merchants; gamblers; travelers; thieves (but only clever, tricky thieves, not thugs or muggers); those who live by their wits; boxers

Manifestation: Hermes traditionally wears a traveler's broad-brimmed hat and sandals

Iconography: Hermes has been through many transitions:

  1. His most ancient images portray him in the form of an erect phallus
  2. He is represented by a cairn of stones
  3. Herms: tall rectangular pillars displaying his head on top and his erect penis sticking out (placed at crossroads; women seeking fertility would place flower garlands around his neck or elsewhere)
  4. A robust man carrying a lamb around his shoulders
  5. Finally: a winged, sandaled, androgynous messenger (most familiar today)

Attribute: Caduceus, a staff entwined by two snakes, the emblem of the modern medical profession. He can use the staff to induce sleep.

Spirit Allies: His mother Maia; Pan; Nymphs

Sacred Sites: Hermes is an extremely unpretentious spirit, among the Greek spirits least often honored with formal temples. Instead he is present at crossroads and in wild nature. Invoke his presence or summon him by erecting a herm or cairn of stones, especially at a four-way crossroads (X-shaped).

Sacred Animals: Dog, tortoise, snake

Tree: Palm

Number: 4

Offerings: Cakes; honey; olives; goat or sheep's cheese; wine; water; incense

Post-Christianity

Hermes as Divine Child wears sandals and carries a staff: his image closely resembles that of the Holy Child of Atocha. Post-Christianity, many of Hermes' functions were assigned to Michael Archangel.

Related Entities

Aphrodite, Asklepios, Athena, Calypso, Carmenta, Circe, Dionysus, Eshu Elegbara, Hades, Hekate, Maia, Mercury, Nymph, Pan, Psychopomp, Shiva, Zeus

Origins in Arcadia

Hermes began his incarnation as a fertility spirit in Arcadia. Born in Mekone, "Poppytown," he has powerful associations with opium, shamanism, and botanical magick. His sacred animals include horned livestock: cows, goats, and sheep. Hermes occasionally takes the form of a horned deity, though by the classical Greek era he was most commonly depicted in his familiar winged messenger form.

Shamanic Guide and Psychopomp

As a master shaman, Hermes is able to travel between the realms of the living, the dead, and spirits. His role as psychopomp includes:

  • Serving as guide when Orpheus traveled to Hades to rescue Eurydice
  • Escorting Persephone as she travels between Life and Death
  • Acting as spell master, providing Odysseus with the antidote against Circe's magick

Patron of Thieves and Cleverness

Hermes is Patron of Thieves and Tricksters but also protects devotees against tricks and theft. He famously enjoys cleverness and despises violence, only protecting non-violent criminals, those using wit, not brawn.

Hermes as Horned God

Hermes is among those spirits classified as horned gods, though his myth is so extensive that he transcends such classification. That Hermes is considered a horned spirit might surprise many: the Hermes of Classical myth is invariably depicted as a man dressed in a uniform of traveler's hat and winged sandals.

Originally, however, Hermes was a deity from rural Arcadia. He began his incarnation as a deity involved with human and agricultural fertility. He is the Lord of Flocks and is often depicted carrying a young lamb or kid, both horned animals.

Like many horned gods, Hermes carries a stick: in his case, it's the caduceus, a short staff entwined by two serpents, still the emblem of the medical profession. He often carries a large bag, too, from which he dispenses gifts and treasures. Hermes frequently limps and is sometimes described as missing one sandal.

Hermes is the father of the goat-god Pan. According to myth, Pan's mother was horrified by the goat-child she bore but Hermes was delighted and it was he who raised and protected his son.

Hermes in Magick and Divination

In addition to shamanism and botanical spells, Hermes sponsors other aspects of magick:

  • As Hermes Trismegistus he was identified with alchemy and ceremonial magick
  • He is the model for the mountebank, the traveling conjurer who may be a true magus, a master illusionist, a charlatan, or all or any of the above
  • Hermes, dressed in his traveler's cap, formed the prototype for the Tarot card The Magician

Hermes as a Boundary God of the Oikos

Within Hellenic household worship, Hermes is one of three Gods who guard the Oikos from outside threats, working alongside Hekate and Apollo Agyieus. His station is at the threshold of the home and just outside its perimeter fence, taking the same office He holds along the road: the herm, the upright pillar that fixes the limits of a place.

Where space allows, the household sets a niche beside the doorway for His herm together with the smaller working tools of the rite, the incense burner and the offering bowl among them. In a modern apartment, a shelf or ledge takes the place of the fence niche. Devotional images here should be three-dimensional, statues or carvings rather than flat pictures, which are reserved for ordinary household decoration.

Daily practice is uncomplicated. Outside of specific sacred days it consists of a simple offering and the burning of incense whenever the practitioner enters or leaves the home.

The Mercury Connection

The word Mercury shares its root with the Latin mercator, meaning merchant, underlining his domain over trade, commerce, and the movement of goods, money, and information.

The Emerald Tablet

Hermes Trismegistus is credited with the Emerald Tablet, the cornerstone of the Great Work in alchemy. Written in deliberately oblique language, the Tablet admits of several interpretations and has been pondered by philosophers and alchemists for centuries. Hermes brings attention to the great mysteries, and also provides the means by which those mysteries may be unravelled.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household economy of offerings, Hermes receives tongue-shaped tokens, rosemary, frankincense and styrax incense, and the wood or branches of the almond and pine. Mint is reserved for His chthonic aspect, Hermes Khthonios. His tokens are the Caduceus, the winged sandals, and the shepherd's flute. His colours are saffron and gold. Sacred animals include the cow, ram, hawk, turtle, and hare; wild strawberry (purslane) and saffron stand among His sacred plants.

Shrine to Hestia

Hestia, known to the Romans as Vesta, is the preeminent goddess of the hearth. Her Roman name may derive from a root meaning "to burn," and as Vesta she played a far more significant role in Rome than Hestia did in Greece, venerated in Italy long before the Greek identification was made.

Preferred Places

  • Home

Preferred Vocations

  • Homemaker

Domains & Sacred Objects

  • Fire
  • Hearth

Ritual Role

Vesta was included in virtually every Roman sacrifice. She was consistently the last deity invoked during ceremonies, the polar opposite of Janus, who was always first.

Temple

Her small circular temple in the Roman Forum stood at the epicenter of Roman life and religion. Its round shape recalled the earliest Romans' huts.

The Vestal Virgins

Vesta was ultimately the only Roman deity served exclusively by a female priesthood. Six Vestal Virgins were chosen in childhood by the Pontifex Maximus from noble families, an exceptional honor. They possessed many legal and economic privileges but also faced severe restrictions and penalties. Service lasted thirty years: ten learning the Mysteries, ten in active service, and ten training replacements. They were sworn to celibacy, though permitted to marry after completing service. If a Vestal broke her vow, she was scourged and buried alive; her lover was whipped to death. The Vestals were considered so sacred that if one walked past a condemned man, he was instantly pardoned.

The Sacred Flame

The Vestals' primary duty was ensuring Rome's sacred flame never went out. If it did, the Vestals were scourged. An extinguished flame could only be relit by rubbing sticks together. The Vestals were also responsible for the mola salsa, sacred ritual salt cakes prepared with water from Juturna's Well, carried in vessels that could not be set down.

Emperor Gratian stopped paying the Vestals' salary between 367 and 378 CE. Rome's sacred flame was finally extinguished in 394 CE when Theodosius banned Pagan devotion.

Home Veneration and Other Powers

Vesta was also venerated in homes and is present in all flames. She is an oracular spirit accessible via flame-gazing. Vesta Powder is a highly combustible occult powder used in her honor and to dispel negativity.

Manifestation

Vesta is rarely depicted and is usually veiled when she is portrayed. She is most commonly represented by fire itself.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within Hellenic tradition, Hestia is the Goddess who granted humanity the gift of the Home, and She stands as the founding divine presence of the Oikos. Her worship holds the highest priority in household life, and its roots reach back into earliest antiquity.

The Goddess and the hearth are identified so completely that they are understood as one and the same. What the hearth is on the physical level, She is on the theological level, and the pair together forms the consecrated heart of the home. The hearth therefore functions as Her primary altar, and the bulk of domestic ceremony takes place at it. The fire burning within represents the Goddess herself in the visible world, and under ordinary conditions it is kept perpetually alight. That flame guards every member of the family, and likewise extends shelter to any outsider who comes to the home seeking refuge.

The institution of EIKESIA, or Supplication, most likely arose by extending this household principle outward to the city. The same rules covering asylum and miasma at the family hearth carried over to the public altar, which strongly suggests that the civic form was modelled on the home.

... for without Thee mortals do not have dinners, where first and last is for Hestia, and begin with libations of sweet wine.

The Communal Hearth

Each Hellenic city maintained its own communal hearth at the sacred core of public life, fulfilling the same role on a civic scale that the household hearth fulfilled at home. The hearth of Athens stood within the Prytaneum, and when settlers departed to establish a new colony they carried fire from it to kindle the hearth of the new city. From that moment the shared flame served as a sacred tie binding colony to mother city.

The hearth also represents an individual household within the surrounding community. To destroy it is to destroy the household, and the consequences fall across many generations, reaching from the forefathers to descendants not yet born, all bound together through the household hearth and the practice of Household Worship.

Prayers and Hearth Phrases

Household rituals typically open with a prayer addressed to Hestia, and the same custom carries through to many communal ceremonies. The practice is preserved in the expression "ΑΦ' ΕΣΤΊΑΣ ΑΡΧΕΣΘΑΙ" ("take your lead from the hearth"), which marks any beginning made in this manner as deeply auspicious.

Conduct at the hearth itself calls for modesty and ritual cleanliness. Appearing before it in a defiled or immodest state violates proper behaviour toward the Goddess.

Rekindling the Sacred Flame

The hearth flame is normally never permitted to die. When death or miasma touches the household, or when certain yearly festivals require it, a ceremony of rekindling is performed. The new fire is drawn either from the central civic hearth or from an undefiled sanctuary, which restores continuity with the broader sacred order.

Correspondences

Emblem: flame. Element: fire. Animal: ass. Mineral: saltpeter. Tree: bay laurel.

Sacred Dates

  • Vestalia (9 to 15 June): Her sanctuary was opened exclusively to women, who entered barefoot. The 15th was a cleaning day; dirt was disposed of in the Tiber.
  • 1 March: The first day of the Roman year, when her flame was ritually relit.
  • Vernal Equinox: Bay laurel branches were discarded.

Offerings and Tokens

Household offerings to Hestia consist of various fragrances of incense. Her tokens are fire, the altar, and the veil. Her colour is white.

The Dark-Haired One

Poseidon is the lord of the sea. Whitecaps are his horses. He lives in an underwater palace and owns all the ocean's treasures. Poseidon is a tempestuous spirit who competes aggressively with Athena for veneration and devotees. According to Olympian myth, Poseidon is the oldest son of Rhea and Kronos.

Scholars suggest that he predates the Olympic pantheon. Poseidon was already a local spirit when incorporated, as opposed to out-of-towner Zeus.
  • He may be an older Greek deity incorporated into the Olympic pantheon like Hera or Demeter
  • Herodotus thought Poseidon was a Libyan deity adopted by the Greeks, possibly like his frequent rival Athena
  • Poseidon may be associated with the earliest Aryan invaders of Greece who entered the region circa 2000 BCE, conquering with horses and wheeled vehicles

Horse Deity Before Ocean Deity

Waves are described as resembling horses, but Poseidon may have been a horse deity before he was an ocean deity. Poseidon taught people how to bridle horses. Chariot races were held in his honor. (The Isthmian aquatic games were also held in his honor.) Poseidon in the guise of a stallion raped his sister, Demeter, in the guise of a mare. (Demeter may have been his original consort.) Their son Arion is a horse. Pegasus, the winged horse, is the child of Medusa and Poseidon.

Poseidon is the ruler, founder, and divine ancestor of the lost continent of Atlantis, whose first king was Poseidon's son Atlas.

Aggressive with Women

Poseidon is aggressive with women. His modus operandi is rape and abduction. In addition to his official consort, Amphitrite, those assaulted by Poseidon include Demeter, Salamis, Melantheia, Peirene, and possibly Medusa. (Sex with Medusa may or may not have been consensual, depending on myth.) All bear his children, indicating his powers as a fertility spirit. Poseidon is invoked for fertility, abundance, and protection at sea. He is a powerful deity and can fulfill virtually all desires. Many of Poseidon's functions were reassigned to Saint Nicholas.

Manifestation

He may manifest as a vigorous, bearded man, a merman or a horse.

Attribute

Spirit Allies

Poseidon often travels accompanied by Amphitrite, their son Triton, and an entourage of Nereids and dolphins.

Creature

Sacred Site

Among others, Poseidon and Amphitrite shared a sanctuary on the Greek island of Tenos famed for its healing miracles. The Church of the Annunciation at Tenos is built over the foundations. The sacred spring within the precinct remains renowned for miracles. The church is filled with ex-votos and testaments to miracles received.

Rituals

Bull fights, boxing matches, and horse races were held in Poseidon's honor.

Mount

His chariot is pulled by horses or hippocampi; sometimes Poseidon rides a hippocampus (a mer-horse) or a dolphin.

Altar

Decorate his altar with marine and equine images.

Roman Neptune

Although Neptune is now considered the Roman Lord of the Sea, he was originally a freshwater spirit of Italy. His associations with the ocean derive entirely from his identification with Poseidon. The identities of the two originally distinct spirits are now so intertwined that their names are used interchangeably. Little information survives regarding Neptune prior to this identification. However, we know that the Romans invoked Neptune to protect fresh water, especially for agricultural uses. His Roman feast day, the Neptunalia, was celebrated on July 23 with feasting and games held in his honor.

Role in Hellenic Household Worship

Within the household pattern of offerings, Poseidon receives horse-shaped tokens, the bull, sea anemone, and myrrh incense. His token is the trident. His colour is cyan. The bull, the dolphin, and the horse stand as His sacred animals, and pine as His sacred plant.

Magickal Properties

The Morrigan is a powerful spirit of birth, death, sex, destruction, and fertility. She is among the goddesses associated with Ireland's well-being and sovereignty. Her name is variously translated as "Great Queen," "Sea Queen," "Phantom Queen," or even "Terrifying Queen." She is an oracular, prophetic spirit who can reveal the future and anyone's destiny, that is, if she feels like it. The Morrigan is a headstrong, passionate goddess who does as she pleases. She is among those goddesses serving as Washers at the Ford.

The Morrigan may be one spirit, a triple goddess (a trinity: three manifestations of one), or name a triad of distinct goddesses, usually Badbh, Nemain, and Morrigan, but sometimes Macha is included.

Ritual Uses

The Morrigan is most famous as a war goddess. She may instigate battle or meddle with it. The concept of minding her own business does not exist: Battle is her business. Anything that captures her interest is her business. The Morrigan is also renowned for giving sound battle advice. She advised the Dagda on how to deal with the Fomorians.

The Morrigan determines war's outcome, bestowing victory to whichever army or warrior she favors, but she has a reputation for being capricious. Her favors can never be taken for granted. Her frenzied war-fury unnerves armies. Her shriek is deadly.

More than just a battle goddess, the Morrigan is also a goddess of life, birth, and sex. She is sometimes identified as a mermaid. On Samhain, the beginning of the Celtic dark half of the year, the Morrigan stands astride a river with one foot on either bank to engage in the Great Rite (sacred, transformative, ritual sex) with the Dagda (Ireland's All-Father).

Offerings

Oatmeal, porridge, mead, Irish whiskey, poteen. Honor her at Samhain.

Victory in battle, prophecy and divination, fertility, transformation, protection in war, sovereignty.

The Morrigan is capricious. Her favor is never guaranteed. Her frenzied war-fury terrifies armies, and her deadly shriek can kill. She does as she pleases and anything that captures her interest becomes her business.

Additional Notes

Her many manifestations include, but are not limited to: a beautiful woman, a hag, a crow, a deer (doe or stag), a white heifer with red ears and no horns, a black eel long enough to coil three times around the legs of Cu Chulain (a giant man).

The Morrigan owns a herd of enchanted, magical cattle. Her sacred birds are corvids: crow, raven, rook. Her sacred color is red. Her sacred day is Samhain (the night of 31 October and 1 November).

Caring for Your Magick Tools

A guide to storing, cleansing, acquiring, and displaying your sacred implements.

What is an Altar?

If you do not have a dedicated altar, or if your altar is not suitable for casting spells, a flat surface such as a table, desk, or counter can be substituted. What matters is that you have a clean, stable workspace for your magickal practice.

Storage and Protection

How do you protect your expensive jewelry? Your heirloom silverware? Your favorite designer clothes? Devote the same care to storing your magick tools.

If you have an altar, you may wish to display your tools on it. Many witches, however, prefer to store their tools safely out of sight, partly to prevent other people from handling them and partly to avoid uncomfortable questions.

Traditional Storage Methods

  • Silk wrapping: Protects from dust, dirt, and ambient vibrations
  • Velvet pouches: Soft protection with elegant presentation
  • Wooden boxes: Natural material that won't interfere with energy
  • Dedicated drawers, trunks, closets, or cabinets: Secure and private

Like any precious possession, you want to safeguard your tools from damage and keep them from falling into the wrong hands.

Precautions and Protocols

When caring for and working with your magick tools, remember these guidelines:

Handling

  • Don't let others use or handle your tools, except perhaps a magickal partner with whom you work regularly
  • If someone touches a tool, smudge or wash it to remove their energy

Divination Decks

  • Use a different tarot deck for reading others than for reading yourself
  • Keep a third deck for spells
  • The same goes for rune sets

Cleansing

  • Clean and smudge all tools before you begin using them for magick
  • After initial cleansing, you needn't cleanse again unless someone else handles them
  • Always wash chalices and cauldrons used for food or drink before storing

Purpose

  • Use your tools for working magick only, not for mundane purposes
  • Treat your magick tools with care and respect, and they'll serve you for a lifetime

Acquiring Magick Tools

When you buy a car, you want to know something about its history. The same holds true for magick tools.

New Items

  • Check out the seller's reputation
  • Get information about the craftspeople who made the objects
  • Read users' reports online

Vintage and Antique Items

Tracking down pedigrees can get tricky. Antique chalices and swords may be exquisitely beautiful, reflecting a level of craftsmanship rarely seen today. However:

⚠️
Energy Warning: Magick tools used by someone else may hold that person's energy for a long time. This is especially true if the objects contain gemstones. Always check your tools' histories if possible before using them.

Cleansing, purifying, and consecrating practices can remove old energies, but knowing the history first is always wise.

Crafting Your Own

You can fabricate your own magick tools if you have skills in woodworking or metalsmithing.

Wands from Wood:

  • Choose a branch that has fallen naturally from the tree (perhaps in a storm or as part of aging)
  • Or request permission from the tree to cut a twig
  • After cutting, make an offering to the tree as thanks

Personalizing Purchased Items:

Even if you buy new items from a metaphysical store, you can add personal touches:

  • Use special paints from craft stores to decorate glass
  • Add meaningful images and symbols
  • Make your tools uniquely yours

Displaying Your Tools

Some witches like to display their primary tools on their altars, alongside:

  • Candles for illumination
  • Statues or deity representations
  • Items required for particular spells or rituals
  • Food and drink offerings
  • Book of shadows

Space Considerations

Things can get crowded on an altar. You're free to move items around as needed:

  • Set up a secondary altar
  • Create four shrines within your sacred space (one for each direction/element)
  • Do whatever you find comfortable and convenient
⚖️
Balance Tip: If you choose to leave your primary tools out on your altar, be sure to display all four for balance—wand, athame, chalice, and pentacle.

Etymology and Symbolism

The word cauldron is related to words indicating heat or to warm up. The English word is believed to derive from the Latin caldarium, meaning "hot bath."

Cauldrons metaphorically represent the female generative organs: the womb, uterus, and vagina. In old Egyptian hieroglyphics, the sign indicating "woman" was a pot. Cauldrons and pots signify the universal womb.

Cauldrons are mythically identified with birth and resurrection. Like a womb, the cauldron reproduces the birth process.

Celtic Mythology

Cauldrons are consistent motifs in Celtic mythology, each possessing unique powers:

The Cauldron of Bran the Blessed is the cauldron of resurrection and rebirth. Bran is the Lord of the Dead; ravens are his sacred bird. He resurrects the dead in his cauldron. Shamans are "cooked" in Bran's cauldron, too (cooking may be understood as transforming raw material).

The Cauldron of Cerridwen brews the potion that confers all wisdom. A cauldron serves as her primary attribute. Her name may derive from a word for cauldron.

The Cauldron of The Dagda leaves no one unsatisfied.

The Cauldron of Diwrnach will not serve a coward.

Branwen is Bran's sister and the star of her own mythic saga. The Cauldron of Resurrection is her marriage dowry.

Associated Spirits and Deities

Medea rejuvenates an old ram in her cauldron; she then converts the cauldron into a murder weapon.

Ogun has among his primary attributes an iron cauldron.

Teutates, an ancient Celtic (Gaulish) deity, drowned humans in his cauldron in the alder groves. Some believe he masquerades as the Grail legend's Fisher King.

Historical and Archaeological Significance

According to Roman writers, cauldrons were used in Teutonic human sacrifice (though as with the Druids, whom the Romans also accused of conducting human sacrifice, this may or may not be true: they were not necessarily impartial observers).

Cauldrons were common grave goods throughout Europe and Asia. Hun graves, for instance, are often identified by their characteristic tall, slim bronze cauldrons.

Bronze and iron cauldrons were deliberately cast into lakes as votive offerings in the British Isles as well as throughout the European continent. Archaeological evidence exists for the ritual depositing of cauldrons in lakes and marshes throughout the last millennium before the Common Era.

Famous Archaeological Finds

The Duchcov Cauldron: A great bronze cauldron filled with over two hundred pieces of bronze jewelry was discovered in Duchcov, Bohemia (now the Czech Republic). The cauldron and its contents, presumed to be an offering to a water deity, were placed in the Giant's Springs—a natural spring that was the focus of much ritual activity during the third century BCE.

The Gundestrup Cauldron: The most famous cauldron is the gilded silver Gundestrup Cauldron, discovered in a peat bog in Gundestrup, Denmark, in 1891. It had been placed on a dry spot within the bog sometime during the first century BCE. The Gundestrup Cauldron is now housed in the National Museum of Copenhagen.

This ceremonial vessel measures three feet in diameter and is constructed from 13 plates, each one bearing repoussé images of deities or mythological scenes. The images include an antlered male deity, deities wearing torcs, and a ram-horned snake.

It is unknown where the cauldron was crafted; scholars suggest that it contains combined Thracian and Celtic elements, perhaps the result of interaction between silversmiths. Some believe it was taken from somewhere in Central Europe and brought to Denmark as war booty.

Spell-Casting Uses

Cauldrons are used for spell-casting. Ancient spells frequently assumed that one had access to a hearth or similar open fire. This is rarely the case nowadays and cauldrons provide the safest substitute.

Greek Love Spell

A Greek spell to conjure up a lover (whether a lost love or a brand new one) suggests that one wreathe a cast iron cauldron with red wool during a waxing moon. Add dried bay laurel leaves and barley grains and burn them within.

Romany Vampire Traditions

Cauldrons rejuvenate: Mullo are Romany vampire-ghosts who return and hover around the living. They may assist their relatives or torment them, however they feel inclined. Among the most feared mullo are those who were stillborn infants.

Once a mullo, always a mullo. A mullo is eternal. Baby mullos are boiled in a cauldron every year on what would have been their birthday by compatriot mullo. This invigorates and rejuvenates them.

Practical Applications

Cauldrons are used to cook brews and potions but are also used to contain fire. A fire may be built within an iron cauldron. Conversely candles may be burned within.

Should one wish to burn candles within a cauldron, it is advisable to spread a layer of clean sand, rock salt, or similar within the cauldron beneath the candles for fire safety and easier clean-up. A lidded cauldron enables you to smother the flames within easily.

Moon Magick

Like Cerridwen's cosmic cauldron of wisdom and transformation, your cauldron is a sacred space for magick and alchemy during lunar workings. It provides a safe vessel for burning herbs, charcoal incense, petition papers, and other offerings aligned to moon phases. Small cast iron cauldrons are widely available at witch supply shops and are well suited to most moon rituals. A lid is especially useful for safely smothering flames when working indoors. Place a fireproof coaster beneath the cauldron during use, as it can become quite hot depending on what is burned inside. A cauldron may not be the first tool a new moon witch acquires, but it becomes invaluable once burning becomes a regular part of your practice.

Triple Legs and Global Symbolism

Traditionally, cauldrons have three legs. The number three here represents the triple aspect of the Great Goddess, or the three Fates. Shakespeare alludes to this when the three Weird Sisters cook up trouble at the beginning of Macbeth.

Magickal cauldrons appear well beyond the Celtic world. In India, a magick life-giving food called Soma was brewed in three huge bottomless cauldrons. In Greece, an ordeal of initiation involved the candidate boiling in a cauldron, emerging after the rite with magickal powers, including the gift of immortality.

Burning Resin Incense

Charcoal discs provide the heat source needed to burn loose resin incenses such as copal, dragon's blood, frankincense, and myrrh. Unlike stick or cone incense, resins require sustained heat to release their fragrant smoke.

How to Use

Place the charcoal disc in a heat-safe container partially filled with sand. Light the edge of the disc and wait for it to spark across the surface, turning gray as it heats. Once the disc is glowing, place small amounts of resin on top. The resin will melt and release smoke.

Safety Considerations

Charcoal discs become extremely hot and will scorch any surface beneath them. Always use a proper censer, cauldron, or heat-resistant dish with sand. Never handle a lit disc with bare hands. Allow discs to cool completely before disposal.

Graveyard dirt is one of the most fundamental and widely used magickal ingredients across traditions worldwide. At its simplest it is soil taken from a cemetery or from a specific grave, though its nature, power, and appropriateness for use varies significantly by cultural framework.

What Graveyard Dirt Is

Graveyard dirt is not inherently malevolent. Whether it is understood as dangerous or benevolent depends on how a given tradition understands the dead. Traditions rooted in African and Asian spiritual frameworks that view ancestral spirits as helpful presences tend to use graveyard dirt for protective and beneficial workings. Traditions that view the dead as threatening or contaminating treat it as toxic power, usable only for cursing.

The term also serves as a nickname for several botanicals with no literal connection to graves:

Valerian is called graveyard dust for its reputation as a sleep aid so powerful it promises sleep like the dead, combined with its distinctly foul smell.

Patchouli is called graveyard dirt for its wet earth aroma.

Mullein shares this name through its associations with Hekate and Oya, two spirits with strong ties to death and cemeteries.

In historical grimoire tradition, graveyard dust could also refer to bone ash mixed with asphaltum, sometimes called mummy dust. This is a rare and archaic usage; the practical modern substitutes are dried powdered mullein or actual churchyard earth.

Some practitioners use one or more of these powdered botanicals in place of actual cemetery dirt. Some combine them with real dirt. Some use only the real thing.

How It Is Collected

Methods vary by tradition and intent. Surface dirt from within cemetery walls is considered sufficient by some. Others dig directly within a grave. British magickal tradition specifies dirt taken from above the heart of the deceased. Hoodoo tradition calls for three scoops: one from above the head, one from above the heart, one from below the feet. ⚠️ Hoodoo is a closed African American folk magick tradition. Research and respect the cultural context before working in this tradition.

When collecting discreetly, a small quantity may be gathered in a pocket or talisman bag. For larger amounts, bringing potted plants to transplant onto the grave is a traditional method: dig a hole for each plant, reserve the loosened dirt, and carry it home in the emptied plant container.

In some traditions, a coin or libation is placed in the hole as payment to the spirit of the grave being disturbed.

Malevolent Uses

The simplest recorded graveyard dirt hex is to throw a handful at the back of a person as they walk away from you. What distinguishes this from a protective toss is not the action but the intent: the practitioner's own suppressed rage and hatred is the active magickal ingredient, and the dirt is merely its vehicle. In Java, graveyard dirt is used to induce unnaturally deep sleep, whether in the context of robbery or unwanted romantic access, preventing others in a household from waking.

Context: Sacred Dirt Across Cultures

Graveyard dirt belongs to a much broader tradition of using earth from significant places as a magickal tool. For centuries, dirt from holy sites and shrines has been carried as protective amulets, placed in graves, sprinkled over sacred objects, or pressed against wounds for healing. Among the most visited examples today is the Shrine of Chimayo in New Mexico, where pilgrims come annually for its reputed healing dirt.

Selecting a Grave for Dark Workings

Graveyard dirt carries different properties depending on whose grave the soil comes from and the purpose of the working. Collecting from the grave of an ancestor is always preferred. When that is not possible, the choice of grave should align with the intent of the spell.

For baneful or aggressive workings, dirt from the grave of someone who died violently or who was a murderer is ideal. If neither is available, dirt from the grave of a child can be used. Ancestral dirt remains a reliable alternative if none of the above are accessible.

Some practitioners consider the full moon the best time to collect, though timing is ultimately a personal decision.

Collecting the Dirt

What to Bring

  • A digging utensil such as a trowel or spoon
  • A container for the dirt (a pill bottle or resealable bag works well)
  • Offerings for the spirit: 9 copper pennies, whisky or wine, and tobacco. If the grave belongs to a child, candy or a small toy is more appropriate.

Scouting the Grave

Visit the cemetery a day before you plan to collect. Choose a grave that feels right. When you return to collect, sit at the grave and meditate. State your purpose clearly and ask if you may purchase the spirit's services. Listen for a reply. If the answer feels like a yes, select from your offerings what you sense the spirit would prefer. If the answer feels like a no, reach out to another spirit who may be agreeable. You will eventually receive a response, or you will feel drawn toward a grave that calls to you.

The Collection

Gather the dirt from the area where you sense the heart would be. If there is grass, carefully remove a plug and set it aside. Dig roughly 3 to 6 inches into the ground and collect your soil. Drop a silver dime into the hole, or copper if you feel the spirit would prefer it. This is your payment. Thank the spirit for the help they are about to provide, then pour whisky, wine, or candy into the hole. Replace the grass plug to cover the site.

Record Keeping

Write down the name, birth date, death date, and the name of the cemetery on a piece of paper or label. Affix it to the container. Hold the bag or bottle of dirt in your hand and pray with conviction for the spirit to accompany you and lend their power through the dirt.

Leaving the Cemetery

Walk away from the grave without looking back. Leave the cemetery by a different route than you arrived. At the cemetery gate, turn around three times, whether on foot or by stepping out of your vehicle to do so. This confuses any spirits that may try to attach themselves to you.

Before entering your home, turn around three more times outside your front door. Be casual about it, as though you are simply surveying the area. Keep a pot filled with many small pebbles and sea salt beside your front door. Add one more pebble before you go inside. Spirits are compelled to try to count the contents, and if they are still counting at sunrise, they are forced to return to the cemetery.

Preparing and Storing the Dirt

The dirt must be dried before use. Two methods work well:

  1. Cloth drying: Tie the dirt, one container's worth at a time, inside an old cotton shirt or dish towel and hang it to dry. Keep batches separate so they do not mix.
  2. Foil drying: For smaller amounts, spread the dirt on a sheet of foil and allow it to dry thoroughly.

Once the dirt is fully dry, sift it. Do this step outside, or wear a mask indoors to avoid breathing in the dust. Separate the material into categories:

  • Fine dust
  • Larger clumps
  • Rocks and pebbles
  • Tiny roots
  • Dead insects

Any live creatures, worms, or insects found during sifting should be placed in a jar and released at the nearest open field.

Store each category in its own labeled jar or bag, all bearing the same name, dates, and cemetery. Keep a notebook logging whom you gathered from, when, and for what purpose. Different components serve different spells; some are better suited for mojo bags or packets, while others work best in powder form.

Every time you use the dirt, call the spirit by name and ask them to assist you by the contract you made at their grave.

Types of Dirt by Source

Mentally Disturbed or Insane Person

Used to cause insanity, mental instability, or psychological unraveling in a target.

Warning: You are dealing with the spirit of someone who was mentally disturbed in life. This energy is volatile and can backlash onto the practitioner.

Murderer or Killer

The older the dirt, the more potent it becomes. Soil from the grave of someone who took human life carries extreme power in matters of revenge and causing harm. Dirt from someone who was hanged is considered especially effective.

Warning: Incorporating this type of dirt into your workings can cause death. Like the dirt of an insane person, this is an unstable energy that demands caution and respect.

A Murdered Person

Highly useful for workings that address injustice or wrongdoing. The spirit's experience of being a victim gives this dirt a sharp edge in matters of retribution on behalf of others who have been harmed.

Nun, Priest, or Pastor

Used when spiritual guidance and spiritual protection are needed. However, some practitioners use this dirt dishonestly to project an illusion of goodness and innocence to the outside world. This is a form of glamoury, and it cannot hold up against someone who is genuinely good.

Oya: Queen of the Dead

Oya holds dominion over all cemeteries. It is essential to gain Her permission before entering Her kingdom. She loves gifts and is not known to have ever turned any down. She is especially fond of red wine and copper. Prepare an old pill bottle with 9 pennies and some red wine as an offering. When you ask Her permission to enter, let Her know you have brought Her a gift.

Knock three times on the ground and speak your incantation before crossing the cemetery threshold. See the full Cemetery Entrance Incantation ritual for the complete protocol.
